speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, March 27, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Usley -Mr. McCann in the chair.

["Mr. Chairman, I have followed with the greatest interest the question of civil aviation ever since the last war, during which eighteen thousand cadets and mechanics of the Royal 'Air Force were trained in the city of Toronto. After the war many prominent people, including the late Colonel Barker, V.C., Air Marshal Bishop, Sir Frederick Handley Page, Air Marshal Collishaw and others came back to Toronto-and as mayor I discussed the matter with them for months-that Canada, which had done so splendidly in the last war, should continue with a programme of civil aviation during the time of peace. As an example, I refer to the progress that had been made three hundred years before on the high seas, when Britain, of her own volition, went out and created an oceanic empire through sea power, when she had only one rival, Portugal, and later on the Dutch. Britain gained command of the sea and built up her magnificent empire.
I am very much disappointed with the secret policy of the government in this connection. Why did Canada not seek first a conference with the other dominions in order to formulate an empire policy as a unit? What was the need for all this secrecy in regard to a public matter such as this, which is of the utmost importance to the future of the world and the future of our empire? Why were all these star chamber proposals made, when w'e had the minister and his staff in London at a time when there were also in that city representatives of nearly all the countries of the world trying to devise some definite plan for the progress of civil aviation and the progress of the world in general? One objection I have to this internationalization of bases is that Russia, our great ally, will have nothing to do with the idea, because they believe in collectivism. The United States will have nothing to do with internationalization; Washington almost shudders when one mentions it and international aviation. They are going to act separately in civil aviation. It is all very well to come here and appeal for this sort of thing, but after all we are only a nation of ten million people. Why should we go outside the empire and make international treaties with these world powers on one of the most important matters ever to come before the people of this country? It is dangerous to plan to share these bases with any other and give them sovereignty, while allowing user. I referred to this matter on July 15 of last year, when the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce were under consideration. At page 4868 of Hansard I said:
If we had had an international policy which meant the giving up of empire ports like Gibraltar and Suez, the Cape, the far east and

the West Indies, where would we be to-day? The empire would have been destroyed, and that would have meant the fall of civilization.
Already we have given the United States bases for ninety-nine years, reaching from Newfoundland to British Guiana, and no doubt they will want to hold on to them. Let us see what that will mean to this country. The bases which it is proposed to share are the backbone of the British empire on the seven seas. Upon them the security of the British empire has depended for some two hundred years, as it will depend in the future. Just fancy what would have happened to the mother country in the present war without these bases! The commonwealths and colonies would be adrift; the empire would become a perfect absurdity on the map; it would be a body without arteries. Just imagine what would have happened in 1940 if we had been compelled to share Gibraltar, Malta, the Cape, Alexandria and these other bases around the seven seas with the United States and Russia, two neutral powers for two years, and all the other powers that were afraid to provoke Germany. Our position would have been impossible. We should have been under pressure to keep neutral. Internationalization presupposes a perfect world of the future. It is one of those dangerous principles. The policy of the government is one of the most dangerous for the mother country that we have had in the last two hundred years. We are prepared to let trusted allies use our bases, as I said on July 15 last-even in peace. But beyond that concession there are dangers. We have to get back and look at the basic principles behind this policy of internationalization. We have to stop and listen, and go back to the very concept of the British nation, united and strong, to defend itself as a unit, existing as an influence among the powers of the world, and ready to cooperate with others on a self-respecting and honourable basis.
Imperial defence should be strengthened. I spoke in the house on July 15 last, after April 2, when the Prime Minister announced the policy which, in my opinion, has prevented an empire conference since then on this important matter of civil aviation. Civil aviation is to be the transport of the future. The Prime Minister practically threw cold water on the whole thing through the following words, which have been quoted in the British House of Commons. He said on April 2:
The Canadian government strongly favours a policy of international collaboration and cooperation in air transport and is prepared to support in international negotiations whatever international air transport policy can be demonstrated as being best calculated to serve not

War Appropriation-Transport
only the immediate national interests of Canada but also our overriding interest in the establishment of an international order which will prevent the outbreak of another world war.
What was the result of that policy, which was quoted in England, in the British House of Commons? In my opinion, it was quoted by the acting leader of the government as one of the reasons why no empire conference on civil aviation should be called. True it is that some time in October, I believe it is the minister and some of his staff went over and had a conference over there. But there were no practical results from that conference. It was said then that under the statute of Westminster each of the dominions is responsible for its home defence, to three miles outside boundary lines. In addition to that, each dominion retains its status, autonomy and sovereignty, and has to look after its own domestic affairs. So much is that so that even in its air policy the domestic policy of Canada is that, following the statute of Westminster we are to set up a vast monopoly in this country, with hidden subsidies, something which will lead to untold error in connection with this work of civil aviation.
I referred to this speech of the Prime Minister when, speaking in the house on July 15 last, I said that the domestic policy of Canada in the air should be based on a well known policy in navigation laws and lease-lend, and that", "We should be ready to cooperate with our allies and allow them to use these air bases, but we should not give away sovereignty over them. The empire has thrown back its enemies from without and in my opinion she will go on to destroy them. Now is the time that we should try to recapture the spirit of empire and our faith and pride in our dominions and in our trade and commerce. The empire is a living thing and should not be allowed to go by default or into liquidation.
That is what you are prepared to do now. You are prepared by this policy to allow this empire to go by default and into liquidation with a war on, instead of being a unit as an empire as to civil aviation. I said further on the same date:
The mother country and the dominions fought this battle alone for two years. Our soldiers carried on with those from India, New Zealand, South Africa, Australia and the empire training plan. We stood shoulder to shoulder in the snows of Labrador and Newfoundland and in the heat of India and the far east.
In the days before the war you could go into any large port and find fifteen or sixteen ships from different parts of the empire carrying on their trade.
I have seen that in Halifax, Victoria and Vancouver.
I believe that this same spirit of empire co-operation will continue in the years that are to come. Canada should be ready to go along
with the dominions and the empire. The time has come when the Minister of Trade and Commerce should tell this committee and the country what our relations are with the other sister dominions who fought along with us for two years to save civilization. One of our great allies stood aside for two years with Germany, but Russia has since made a glorious record. To-day she is practically fighting her battles alone except for some supplies and munitions that are being sent in.
I went on record to the effect that the policy should be to allow these bases to be used by all the world in the future. But sovereignty-no. They should be retained by the mother country and by the British empire. That is why I have objected to such secret policies in the house.
Had the same energy been put into civil aviation in the period between the two wars that has been put into it in the empire air plan since the war started, we never would have had a second war. I have followed this civil aviation question, right from the start of the last war, and I have been very much disappointed in what I have seen.
The minister of Munitions and Supply on the 17th if this month gave a fine history of civil aviation. He placed on record a splendid summary of the progress of civil aviation. He pointed out what had been done by private , enterprise and private initiative. Then he went on to refer to many other matters, pointing out that a reduction had been made in the estimates in 1935, and then went on to a reference to Trans-Canada Air Lines, and how Canadian Pacific Air Lines would not come in.
Did this international agreement he quoted ever come before the other dominions? I am referring to this international agreement given out secretly at Washington, over the heads of parliament, behind our back, when parliament was in iession, which decided on a domestic policy involving the greatest monopoly this country has ever seen, and for the payment of hidden subsidies to a corporation whose civilian heads had had very little training. There was one exception, because the head of Trans-Canada Air Lines, Philip Johnson, had come from the United States, and was an able business man who had had experience in aviation.
But Canada's policy of not calling an empire conference on civil aviation will have unfortunate results, because she has been advocating a policy of internationalization. No definition has been given with respect to what internationalization is, and no one understands what it is. The House of Commons has never seen this particular agreement, and I doubt if some of the dominions have ever
War Appropriation

Transport", 'read it. I doubt if the British parliament has ever seen it or discussed it, because they had a debate over there last June.
Some forip of internationalization is no doubt necessary. Some form of private enterprise, or a mixed form of private and public enterprise, might be considered. But I believe the whole policy of the government is entirely wrong and a leap in the dark, and it is one which will not commend itself to the wisdom of the country. After all is said and done, if that is the view of the government, then there is very little hope for civil aviation in Canada in the future of Canada or the empire. I never have been able to see how this secret conclusion was ever reached. Civil aviation should not be a political question, nor should it be the plaything of any political party. It should be considered on its merits. In the great future which lies before this country we must wrap ourselves up with the mother country and the dominions, as a unit, in a joint empire air scheme, as we did in war.
As far as domestic aviation goes it is wrong to create a monopoly in this and other countries. The government is just drawing red herrings across the track, with a war on, and creating unnecessary dog-fights between these two companies. All this is being done when the war is not yet won. We should get back to basic things, namely, what the British empire as a unit should do in connection with civil aviation with an all-empire plan.
Instead of sticking to the main policy and the main task that is before us, instead of considering what is best to be done, we start off by creating a dog-fight between the two transportation systems in this country which have been doing glorious work in this war.
I was interested in civil aviation many years ago in connection with the policy of the present government and the government before it. Little or nothing was done, before the two wars, about civil aviation; it was left to private enterprise. The means by which we were able to obtain a technical victory in the battle of Great Britain were made possible by the information obtained in the Schneider race in 1931. The British government were able to obtain information which laid the foundations for the winning of the battle of London in 1940. The low-wing monoplane was born in that race, and this was the ancestor of the Spitfire and the Hurricane. Many great inventions followed out of the information obtained from those races. But there has been a complete lack of policy on the part of this government and that of the mother country in connection with civil aviation.

I am dissatisfied with the policy of this government because it will not solve the problem. The two transportation companies are to be put'out of existence in the air and all surface road transport, and a new company is to be substituted. They do not say how Canadian Pacific Air Lines are to be liquidated, and they fail to recognize the findings of the council of British shipping. This is an important body which has done much to help to win the battle of the Atlantic and keep the empire trade routes open in war. Their experience dates back for 200 years in providing sea services, and they outline the part they feel they can play in civil aviation. The report of that body in 1944 reads:
Our problem in this matter is greater, hut our opportunities are also greater than those of any other great power. The shipping industry does not pretend to any specialized knowledge of aviation, but it possesses experience of travel.
What it does possess and what it offers as a practical contribution to this task is a wealth of experience derived from our generations of successful management of overseas services; an efficient organization already dealing with those classes of passengers and freights likely to be borne by air; and a network of branch offices and agencies all over the world.
That contribution, the result of vast experience, W'as at first gained in monopoly before other countries took to overseas ventures, and then in competition with shipping subsidized by foreign governments. Having watched the effects of subsidies and of monopoly, the shipping companies believe that they should not be established for the air. They also believe that "persistent subsidy would retard genuinely healthy progress." ...
The war itself is both a forcing house for the development of the aeroplane and an agent for the wholesale destruction of ships. What might therefore have been a gradual, will become an abrupt transition. British shipowners, when tackling the rehabilitation of their traditional services after the war, will be presented also with an unusual opportunity to convert them spontaneously from the old medium to the new, in whatever respects and in whatever proportions their respective characteristics and the requirements of each trade or group of trades may suggest.
But any such spontaneous conversion is faced immediately by two obstacles. First, there is the risk under present legislation that shipowners may find themselves in competition with their qwn government in the shape of British overseas airways corporation.
This corporation holds a legal monopoly of all British services which are subsidized from public funds. The council of British shipping hold that their experience is of great value to the future.
A far wider and more varied deployment of experience, resources and individual enterprise would appear to be required, and British shipowners, in technique and experience and in their long established position in international transport, should be able to make certainly not

War Appropriation-Transport
an executive but a substantial contribution to the sum total of British air commerce. Ships and aeroplanes are by no means mutually exclusive. On the contrary, experience has shown that they can, and ideally should, be operated in a sense complementary to each other.
The conduct of a regular air line and that of a regular se& line have wholly systematic characteristics. Each calls for long term policies; each requires an international outlook; in each rigid technical discipline is essential to public safety; each finally succeeds only by capturing and retaining the goodwill of the travelling public or the consignor of freight.
In this remarkable memorandum the council of British shipping have made a real contribution to our understanding of the subject of air and sea transport. They end with suggesting that there should be a national empire board and they say;
In its twenty-five years of existence the national maritime board, on all questions of seagoing conditions and pay, has not only acquired confidence and authority, but has developed within itself a happy combination of mutual respect, eommonsense and an absence of rhetoric.
New Zealand and Australia have attempted to do something in connection with air routes and civil aviation. Mr. Curtin and Mr. Fraser appealed to Canada, last January when they met, to hold a meeting in order to bring about a unified policy for the empire. When I spoke on this matter here two weeks ago I quoted the speeches of Mr. Curtin and Mr. Fraser of January last and also referred to what the war correspondent of the Sunday Times said in his dispatch dated January 16. I repeat:
It is not generally realized at home that America has a Pacific air route which is marvellously well organized. On the day after war ends the same pilots, planes, air crews, ground organization, wireless and meteorological services will be available to begin commercial air services between Canada, America, Australia and New Zealand.
The British empire will not be in this lucrative traffic because nowhere on the Pacific route during war is there one British plane, pilot, meteorological expert or radio operator. Unless Britain places air crews on this route in 1944 she will be left at the post as far as experience and good will of services go, if peace comes in 1G45.
The Prime Ministers of Australia and New Zealand made an appeal to Canada to send delegates to an empire conference, and urged that serious consideration be given to the question.
The United States have been progressive in civil aviation. Many of the prominent men in this industry gained their experience in the R.A.F. in Toronto during the last war. The Americans have a tremendous hold over the Pacific, and they did not get it by accident but by enterprise, at a time when Canada
was asleep. They have made great concessions to travellers. The United States air service over the Pacific is free, every military or civilian traveller having the benefit of that route at no cost to himself.
The Prime Ministers of Australia and New Zealand had a conference on the 17th of January at which they agreed on an airways plan and made an appeal for an empire air policy. Canada has ignored it all, and has done nothing about it. Now Canada announces an international air policy as though she were a first-class power. I can tell you this, that America will have nothing to do with internationalization, neither will Russia. Russia has an agreement with the mother country for after the war to which the dominions are not a party.
I am very much disappointed with the whole air policy of the government, and I do not believe it will ever be consummated. In Canada we should have a chair in civil aviation in every large university, especially after the glorious record that Canada has made in this war with the empire training plan, which cost the taxpayers of this country close to a billion dollars. But we shall get little value out of it all under the domestic and international policies of this government. How does it come about that this policy is announced over the head of parliament and that a secret international document like this was produced in Washington over our heads and put into the record? It was done over the head of this parliament while in session, and over the head of the mother country, over the head of Australia and New Zealand and the other dominions which have been fighting with Canada in this war. Imagine the future for our young aviators coming back from this war if we have no settled air policy! This policy has been got up by a minister of the crown over the head of parliament. How many members have read this secret international proposed agreement? I have read it three or four times and I as a simple Canadian citizen am shocked by it. It gees over the head of Britain, which stood alone in the battle of Britain. This policy is got out over the head of parliament while our young aviators are fighting overseas. I doubt if few members have read the policy. It is, in my opinion, a shock to the people of the empire, and I have made a study of civil aviation ever since the magnificent record Canada made in the air in the last war.
I have waited for over twenty years for this day, to see that civil aviation would at least get a break here and that we could have
War Appropriation-Transport', "a discussion in this house of this matter. Hitherto we have had no chance to discuss the future of aviation and the place it will occupy in our life when our young men come back from the war. How many of them, when they return, will have one hundred dollars in their pockets to finance a feeder line? What is the use of talking about their coming home as o-wners to enter an air industry? They will have twenty-five dollars in their pocket to buy a suit of clothes, but not sixty dollars, and yet we have squandered millions on camps all over this country without suitable sewers or water in them. Is that what our pilots are fighting for? Is that what we are doing for them, instead of calling a conference with the other dominions with a view to action along the lines I have indicated?
We have a navigation policy under which any ship can enter our harbours and land its cargo. They cannot enter our coastwise trade on the Atlantic or Pacific, but they can land their goods at our ports. That policy has proven in navigation a success for two hundred years, and has made Great Britain the great ocean-going country she is. The same principle should be applied to civil aviation, which should be free the world over. I regret that, instead of sticking to the large issue, the government has brought in these irrelevant matters when the war is on, and at a time when the railways are doing magnificent work they are to be deprived of any share in civil aviation. At a time when railway facilities in this country are choked, the ministry says: Nobody shall engage in civil aviation except the government, and they shall have a monopoly of it. I am not a Canadian Pacific man or any other kind of man, but one of independent mind, but I do say that this policy is a mistake. The government has got out a political feport on civil aviation in the domestic and in the international field. Civil aviation should rank next ,to agriculture in providing work and employment for our young men when they return from this war after writing the most glorious page in the lpstory of the world. I still have ten to fifteen minutes, Mr. Chairman, and I will continue my remarks when this question comes before us again, since I see it is now eleven o'clock.

It is not my desire to delay the proceedings of the committee but may I say there are two or three important matters which have come before the house during the past year. The ministry have made certain proposals with regard to two or three matters in which I am interested, namely, coal, housing, shipbuilding and one or two others relating to the city of Toronto. The minister made a long statement with regard to the coal question. It is now proposed to appoint another royal commission to go into the whole question of our fuel resources and what is to be done during the remainder of the war and long after the war.
This is not a new question or a new topic. The question of a national fuel supply has been raised on other occasions. I hold in my hand a volume of Hansard for the year 1923. During that year a debate of two or three days' duration took place on a resolution regarding a national coal supply. I brought that resolution before the house on March 19, 1943. In it I asked that the fuel requirements of Canada should be obtained as far as possible from the British empire, from Alberta, the maritimes and Wales. During the debate it was shown that we were sending 850,000,000 a year to Pennsylvania to obtain anthracite coal from the mines there and in that way we were supporting those mines. The proposal was that Canada should establish a system of bonuses, subventions and subsidies in order that our coal [Mr. Senn.l	.
producing provinces may be able to provide us with coal, thereby relieving us from becoming absolutely dependent on a foreign supply of coal from Pennsylvania and other coal producing areas of the United States.
The resolution I proposed at that time was not referred to a royal commission to waste time but was sent to the standing committee on mines and resources. I do not think that committee has held a meeting since the war started. Surely with all the information we have in connection with the problem of a national fuel supply we do not need to send this question to a royal commission. We were fortunate last winter in that we did not have one of the winters that we have experienced in the past when the Canadian people had to fire their furnaces eight or nine months in the year. I remember a few years ago we had to put coal in our furnaces right up to the end of May. There were many other winters just as bad. The government should have formulated a policy long ago. We have heard of meetings with the provinces and the municipalities. As a result of my resolution the government of the day, three or four years late, instituted a policy whereby they paid subventions and subsidies on coal from Nova Scotia to the central provinces. This coal was moved partly by rail and water and all water to the head of the lakes. Hundreds of thousands of tons have been moved by that route in years gone by. Subsidies of a dollar a ton and sometimes more than that, and occasionally less than that, have been paid through the railways by the country.
The production of coal in Alberta is only in its infancy. There was a proposal that we should utilize pipelines for oil and all these things. That started away back in 1923. Little or nothing has been done about it. Inasmuch as it is the poor people who suffer I do hope that something will be done. I should like to refer to the larger cities, and more particularly the city of Toronto. Some
830,000,000 have been spent on the whole waterfront and in the vicinity of Ashbridges Bay to establish facilities for handling coal in that industrial district. Nearly five or six hundred thousand tons of coal are piled in the eastern end of the waterfront in a year. That has helped greatly to relieve the coal situation in that district, but the supply is dwindling. Owing to the strikes and the situation which exists in the United States and the demands of the war we do not know what is going to happen. We do not know whether we are going to have any supply for next winter owing to the changing conditions in that country and the changing war. Where are we to get our substitutes? The other evening the minister referred to a pile of

War Appropriation-Supplies
wood at the head of the lakes. We should like to get some of that wood in Toronto. We understand that during the coming summer barges are going to move that wood to some of the ports down here.
The fuel situation is a world situation. So far as Canada is concerned it depends largely on transportation and the labour situation. I am not going to say very much more on this question but I do hope that some substitutes will be found.
In 1923 I advocated a system of a national hydro policy for this country. It was shown in the returns that were brought down at that time that we had a potential horse-power of
42,000,000 with only about 7,000,000 horsepower developed. Part of it was seasonal, used only in the summer time. Only one sixth or 7,000,000 horse-power had actually been developed. It was shown then that we had not been progressive enough as a country. There should be a further utilization of our hydro resources for heating purposes where possible. There should be a national hydro policy. On my last visit to British Columbia in 1927 I was very much surprised to find that the rich natural resources of waterpower that that province enjoys were not utilized in that way to the extent that they should be in public ownership thereof. We have to do something because before many months are past our fuel supplies will have been exhausted. Many cities and towns are now living from hand to mouth. The control board has brought about more confusion than relief. Delivery is a very important factor to many small dealers in the cities and towns of this country. With the labour situation as it is, particularly in the mines, and with the income taxes which have been imposed on mine workers both here and in the old country, it is difficult for some of the mines I know to secure the proper help. What are w'e going to do next winter? We are not through this winter yet; we seem to be headed for a belated cold spell during the latter part of March and April, which are the most dangerous months for many of the diseases that prevail in this country, such as pneumonia and so on. There is not a day to be lost in getting ready for next fall. The appointment of a royal commission has been announced, but you might just as well save jmur money. I see no reason why the committee on mines, forests and waters should not have been meeting throughout the war dealing with questions of this kind. The fuel situation has been made a political football; it has been discussed by three or four committees and commissions which have called witnesses and made reports. One of these was the 100-121
select committee on reconstruction and security after the war, but I know of no reconstruction which has been brought about in regard to the national fuel policy as a result of the work of these committees. We have the committee on mines; we have three or four departments or branches of departments all interested in the same questions, but nothing seems to be done. I do urge upon the house that this is the most important question we have to face in Canada, especially in connection with the working classes. I do not know how they came through last winter, and no one knows what is going to happen by next September, with our supplies of coal from the United States being curtailed all the time.
Now I should like to say a word with regard to the housing situation. I admit that any discussion of this question is limited to item 3 of the minister's estimates, which deals with housing development in war time, and the amount of which has been reduced to $11,000,-
000.	I would remind hon. members, however, that last Sunday evening the Prime Minister of Great Britain set a goal of 500,000 prefabricated houses for the returned soldiers and working people of his country, and I imagine that actually nearly a million homes will be required. Why are we not doing something about housing in a practical way? We appointed a rent controller, but he has simply tied up real estate in a worse knot than ever, with the result that now no one in the cities and towns wants to own real estate. With all the artificial burdens and barriers placed on home ownership it amounts practically to the confiscation of real estate. According to the assessment commissioner of Toronto, when war broke out over sixty per cent of the people of that city owned their own homes. I believe the latest figures indicate that at a conservative estimate more than one hundred thousand people have been driven from their small homes into apartments. When the war is over these people will want to find small houses in which they may live with their wives and families. Many of these houses will be required by returned soldiers. I understand that according to a recent survey in Toronto some sixteen thousand families will have to find new homes on May 1, and many of them are the families of soldiers who are now overseas. I have some of them in my own constituency, which was referred to in the report on housing prepared under the direction of Lieutenant-Governor Bruce away back in 1934.
I believe the Prime Minister of Great Britain has said on many occasions, in connection with this housing problem, that homes

War Appropriation-Supplies

built during the war should be of such style and construction, and contain such appliances and improvements, as will enable them to fit into the scheme of things when the war is over. Away back on January 24, 1935, I moved a resolution in this house regarding the housing situation and the construction industry. It brought about a very thorough investigation by a committee of the house which sat for some five months, heard witnesses and made a report to parliament. This is the resolution I moved:
That in the opinion of this house Canada should inaugurate at once a national housing, building and reconstruction policy adapted to its circumstances, and that such a policy is an economic and social necessity and in the best interests of the people of our country.
The debate on that resolution lasted well into the evening, when Mr. Bennett, who was then prime minister, proposed the appointment of a select committee to go into the question. That committee recommended the construction of a large number of small houses. I was a member of the committee; we heard witnesses from all over the world, and the report is just as applicable to-day as it was then. When the present government came in they adopted the suggestion I had made in the committee, that instead of the government creating a large housing department the work should be done by private industry and loans made through the banks. I want to give hon. gentlemen opposite a great deal of credit for what has been done in that connection. Some $83,000,000 has been invested in small homes, with the banks loaning the money and the loans guaranteed by the government. These small homes were well constructed on standard plans at low cost; you can see them all over the city of Toronto now, and they are a credit to the present government and to Mr. Bennett, who supported the scheme.
I wish to help the minister; I do not want to sit here as a private member of the opposition and raise unnecessary objections, because I know what this war business means. I have seen two great wars, and I know the difficulty of carrying on, but I do say that in connection with the housing situation we have had too many people taking a hand, too many committees, too much red tape and too few houses being built. We should get down to some system along the lines suggested by Mr. Churchill the other evening, under which we will provide houses for soldiers and civilians. I would not say twenty-five thousand houses in the Toronto district would be enough; I do not think that number would meet the situation at all, but I think we should do something before we adjourn for Easter, because on May 1 a great many people

will be put out by the bailiff. People do not want to own houses to-day, with all the controls that are in existence. You cannot get enough revenue to pay the taxes and interest on the investment, let alone the depreciation, so you make nothing out of the property. In many cases real estate has become a burden because of excessive taxation.
We will have to get down to brass tacks and decide three things in regard to housing and reconstruction. First, what is Canada going to do to see that the industries of this country furnish a large share of the building materials and supplies which Britain will need for the manufacture of these half a million prefabricated homes proposed by Prime Minister Churchill last Sunday evening? We will have to come to a decision in regard to tariffs. What is to become of preferential trade within the empire; what is to become of favoured nation treaties? We have the cart before the horse in appointing these committees; we have to solve these other problems first. Are we going to get the large share we should get in connection with the construction of these homes in the old country and, if so. how is it going to be done? I say to my hon. friends to the left that they have to give the Conservative party credit for a great many things which have been done in the city of Toronto, though of course the Liberals also and others were equally active in public ownership there. Toronto was the pioneer and leader in many of these advances; by its guaranteeing of bonds it financed seventy-five per cent of the initial hydro cheap light, power and transportation programme under which the city went into the building of roads outside the city, purchased the street car lines, gave an improved water supply, developed a fine harbour and provided facilities so that coal could be brought from lake Ontario and lake Erie ports, and in fact right to Mr. Baldwin's own plant in Ashbridge's bay from Swansea, Wales, in 1915-16. . During that period many services in transportation were extended to the counties of Ontario and Peel, where my hon. leader lives, by purchase of the radials and by new buses; in fact Toronto took the lead in supplying transportation and other services through the Toronto Transportation commission throughout the area.
What has been done there? We have a housing situation, a coal situation, and a situation respecting improved roads. I do hope something will be done about it. Sometimes the committee on reconstruction seems to be away up in the clouds. It seems never to get down to terra firma. It never gets down to the ground to discuss how houses are to be built so as to house these 16,000 people who are to be out of their homes on

War Appropriation-Supplies
the first of Maj'. Nothing is being done to provide for those among them who may be soldiers.
Sometimes it is and sometimes it is not advisable to criticize the government of the day. But it is a function and a duty of the opposition to criticize, and it is certainly a duty to criticize when we find that when faced with this situation the government does not do anything. We shall have to decide about these problems before very long. So far the government has put the cart before the horse in what it has done. However, this coal and housing question is a world problem.
There is one other matter to which I should like to refer. Some hon. members seem to be able to discuss civil aviation, while others are not allowed to do so. The whole field of civil aviation and its proper solution should be discussed. I believe the leader of the opposition deserved a great deal of credit for his decision that the opposition should give thorough study to the matter before coming to any definite conclusion. I understand an agreement has been reached over parliament's head, as to both domestic and international aviation. For twenty years I have studied the matter, and I believe that before the imperial conference is held some policy should be decided. I shall not discuss it now, because no doubt an opportunity will be given later. But I do believe there should be a discussion before the imperial conference is held. The high court of parliament is meeting, and we must have something to say about it. There was a statement by the prime minister on April 2, 1943, which, in effect, is the gist of the proposals of the present minister on civil aviation with respect to domestic and international affairs. I believe at some other time we should have an opportunity to discuss this matter, and a time should be set aside for the purpose. We should go into all aspects of it, because it is a very involved question. I remember at the close of the last war discussing it with the late Colonel Barker, V.C., and Sir Frederick Handley Page, who came t'o our city. More than twenty years passed between the two wars; Canada left it to private initiative and forgot all about it. In my view something should be done about it. I do not see why my friends to the left should be permitted to discuss a matter of this kind, while others have to wait until a later time.
A large shipbuilding industry was brought to our city in 1917. At that time I was one of the heads of the harbour development. I remember discussing with the late Mr. Hazen, then minister of marine and fisheries, the matter of shipbuilding in Toronto. At that 100-121i
time a large number of wooden ships were built. One of those ships was of about 9,000 tons. I hope the minister will do something so that wooden ships may be built on the great lakes. The government has spent about
S125,000,000 on the deepening of the Welland canal and the improvement of inland waterways in Canada. In view of the coal situation, and many other matters of that kind, I believe the time has come when some of these plants should be converted to peace-time plants, and that the government should consider establishing a system whereby wooden ships would be built to carry the traffic on the inland waterways and coastal traffic along the Atlantic coast after the war.
In 1917 one of those ships was named after me, but unfortunately in 1939 it was sunk on the Atlantic by the Germans three or four days after it put to sea, after the Athenia was lost. I am not much good at having things named after me, because when I was head of the municipality and the Toronto Transportation commission was started to take over the street railway, it was decided that they be called the Toronto Civic Lines. But after the matter was considered I told them they had better not use that name, because sometimes they might be called Tommy Church's lines-which they were, more or less,
I may say.
But I do say to the government that all along the great lakes it should get ready for the close of the war, and have these shipbuilding industries established, if we are to be ready for the great trade which will flow to this country after the war by means of water-borne traffic and shipment by rail.
These are the only suggestions I have, and I hope the minister will consider some of them. I should like to see something of a practical nature done immediately along these lines before the end of the war.

It would seem that some of the ministers are not completely informed at the moment respecting certain details. For this reason I draw to the attention of the minister an item which appeared in the Alaska Weekly, published at Seattle, Washington, on Friday,

March 17, 1944, which, I believe, throws some light oa the matter under discussion. This item, under an Ottawa dateline, states:
A vast bloc of territory in the Canadian northwest, including all the Yukon Territories comprising nearly 1,000,000 square miles, has been set aside as an oil reserve for exploration and drilling exclusively by the United States War Department for the duration of the war.
This has been disclosed in official documents relating to the Canol project and other military developments involving United States expenditures in northern Canada.
This, I think, is the important point in the dispatch, and the one concerning which the hon. member for Yukon expressed more than usual interest:

I should like to refer to one matter which I do not think has been discussed up to now. I do not see any place where it might properly be discussed later. I refer to the distribution of lumber in the western provinces. It has been brought to my attention, and I have observed myself, that there is a situation developing throughout Canada which is proving to the disadvantage of certain types of lumber dealers. I refer to the independent dealer. There seems to be a distinct difference between the position of the independent dealers and that of the line companies. My own observation has been that the independent lumber dealer cannot get lumber, while the line companies, perhaps 
because of better connections or something of the kind, seem to be able to get substantial supplies.
In certain communities there is only the one type of dealer, the independent, and the result is that the farmers in those communities are unable to secure lumber for repair work or for the building of granaries and so on. In other communities where line companies are operating they are able to obtain the lumber they require. I do not know whether it is the fact, but complaint is made that the suppliers of lumber are more interested in exporting to the United States than they are in supplying the local market, particularly in the western provinces. Another claim made is that dealers, particularly the independent dealers, are being forced to take off-sizes, boards of the wrong widths, and dimension stuff which is not suitable for their operations.
The lumber dealers are concerned about the situation. Many have spoken to me and pressed for a clarification. Is the minister in a position to tell us just what the situation is with respect to the supply of lumber or the controls that are operating, particularly the controls that affect the independent dealers and the line companies?

The problem referred to by my hon. friend has been receiving the continuous attention of the timber controller for a good many months and every effort has been made to provide adequate supplies of lumber all over the prairies. The difficulty has been to obtain proper distribution. My hon. friend is quite right when he says that the producers of lumber are interested in getting export prices. As hon. members know, prices within Canada are governed by price ceilings, while those across the line are much higher. There has been some trouble with producers cutting lumber to sizes suitable for the export market and unsuitable for the Canadian market. The timber controller in these cases has ordered the lumber recut, and I think the practice referred to is being broken down,
As my hon. friend knows, lumber is cut in the northern part of the three prairie provinces, and the problem has been to get good distribution in the southern part where freight charges are higher. A procedure has been adopted which I think has worked out in the main. Out of four cars produced, a producer may sell two where he likes, and if he ships the third into the southern part of the province as directed by the timber controller he *may export the fourth car. That is an arbitrary rule but I think it has worked out fairly well.

War Appropriation-Supplies
We have been informed by reliable sources in Saskatchewan during the past two or three weeks that there is sufficient lumber on the prairies, and requests have been received from there to permit a greater volume of exports. However, the timber controller is not satisfied that there is sufficient lumber on the prairies. and this request has not been acceded to. I think the situation has improved. I see no reason why local yards cannot buy as freely as the line companies, because the transactions are between the producer and the retailer. I shall be glad to have my officers make inquiries to see whether there is a real difficulty, and if there is, to take steps to overcome it.

It appears that these people generally buy through brokers, but now that lumber is in a tight position the larger outfits are buying direct and short-circuiting the commission men. The result is that certain dealers cannot get any lumber at all while others are short-circuiting the regulations. Is the minister in a position to state the approximate quantity of lumber that will be available to the western provinces during the coming season?
I am afraid I cannot give the figures. I shall look up that information and try to have it before we finish this evening.

Will the minister also
inquire about the quality of lumber being distributed in western Canada as compared with the quality of the lumber being shipped to the United States? We have found that the quality of lumber has deteriorated seriously during the last two or three years. Apparently they are exporting the better grades of- lumber and leaving the poorer quality for the home market, which is not altogether fair.
I shall be glad to look into that.

I should like to make a few remarks about the shipbuilding industry. We are very much interested in this industry in the province of Quebec and we have made a considerable contribution toward the success of the war in this connection. Our riveters have set up some fine records, but these workers are beginning to wonder what is going to happen in the future. Are we going to have a merchant marine worthy of an independent and strong Canada?
The minister stated that by March 1 we had completed fifty-four 10,000-ton ships, including ten tankers and thirteen 4,700-ton ships, and that these had been delivered to
the Park Steamship company. He also estimated that by the end of August an additional thirty 10,000-ton ships, including three tankers, would be added to the Canadian merchant fleet. Therefore by the end of August the Park Steamship fleet will consist of the following: 71 dry cargo vessels of 10,000 tons; 13 tankers of 10,000 tons; 13 dry cargo vessels of 4,700 tons.
The dry cargo fleet will approximate about three-quarters of a million tons dead weight. The minister admits that the 4,700-ton vessels are useful only in the coasting trade. The 10,000-ton vessels, even the Canadian Victory ships, are of a type that will be in tremendous oversupply after the war. They will be utterly unable to compete with the United States, British and other foreign vessels. The Canadian Victory ships are slow-I am informed they can make only ten to eleven knots at best-and are not to be compared with the United States ships of the same name which are of an entirely different type. These United States ships have a speed of from sixteen to eighteen knots and are now being turned out in United States yards in large volume for use both during the war and in the post-war period. The Canadian Victory ship compares with the American Liberty ship, which is now generally known to have little post-war value. Why did we in Canada not turn to the production of a more useful type of vessel for post-war trade, especially as the yards have been cutting down production?
I read a statement in the report of the Canadian Pacific Railway company that they have ordered a number of ships of the Beaver type in England. I do not know the exact speed of these ships; could the minister give it? The recently announced reconstruction programme of the United States Maritime commission for the year beginning next July includes 213 C-type ships whose speed will be faster than that of the Victory ships; 1,131 Victory ships, 372 tankers and only 194 Liberty ships. Other types make up a total of 2,359 ships. The fact is that in the United States they are concentrating on the faster ship, the Victory ship and the C-type ship. But we are to have only slow ships and I am very much afraid they may be useless. We shall only be able to operate them as tramp vessels carrying cargoes at bargain rates, and there will always be arguments over the wages paid on such ships, because it will be said they take so much longer to complete a trip, and the tendency will be for wages on these ships to be lower. We have still time to correct the situation. It is true that we must
War Appropriation-Supplies



build as many ships as are required for victory, but other countries, while producing ships for victory, have also in mind the postwar and are preparing for it by building a faster type of ship. The picture I am painting does not appear to be very bright, but these are the facts.	-
An article in the Shipping World of December 22, 1943, points out that before the war there were about 10,000,000 tons of tramp shipping and that that figure would be increased easily to 21,000,000 at the end of the war. Of that total, 5,000,000 tons will be privately-owned and the rest government-owned. The figures are as follows: United States government, 12,000,000 tons; Canada,
2,000,000 tons; United Kingdom, 1,500,000 tons; continental governments, 500,000 tons. The United States and other countries will have plenty of fast tonnage, and if necessary they will do away with the tramp tonnage altogether, while we shall be left with nothing but tramp tonnage.
An article in the London Economist of January 1, 1944, points out that any large scale selling of these ships by the government to private owners would push the bottom out of the freight market as effectively as an attempt by the government to keep these vessels in operation.
I repeat that I am not raising this issue to argue that it was not necessary at a certain time to build the kind of ship we have as rapidly as possible to carry supplies and munitions of war to the armed forces. But we have reached the stage where we must think of the future, and it is only right that Canada should have a government-owned merchant marine. We had one in the past, the C.G.M.M. They were old ships, and we must have better in the future. We should have shipping to be prepared for any emergency. We have the trained men, and we ' should build up a merchant marine that the Canadian people can be proud of. Young and old would be proud to see a fast fleet of Canadian government merchant vessels flying the flag of their country; and I hope that our ships will fly a truly Canadian flag.

Mr. Chairman, I notice that the first item of the minister's estimates provided the sum of $195,000,000 as the estimated requirements for 1943-44, for additions and extensions to plants with estimated expenditures for 1943-44 of $149,033,690.74, and estimated requirements for 1944-45 of $60,000,000. I would like the minister to give the details of these expenditures as completely as he can.
I Mr. Rose.]
I do not wish to enter into another discussion with respect to the maritime provinces; I think our position is pretty well understood. I want to express my appreciation of what has been done in developing some industries in the maritime provinces during the war, although only a small portion of the war expenditures have been spent in the maritime provinces. It is recognized by the people of the maritime provinces, and I think by people all over Canada, that the maritime provinces and the outlying portions of Canada have not shared in the war expenditures as they should share if there is to be equality of industrial development in Canada. This is unfair to the west, but much more so to the maritime provinces, inasmuch as the west never had established industries, while the maritimes had scores and scores of industries which no longer exist or exist only as very small establishments. They have been absorbed by industry in central Canada or have been crowded out by mass production and mass merchandising. There never was a better opportunity given to a government than during the war years to restore an equilibrium of industrial enterprise in Canada by establishing industries in the maritime provinces. These enormous expenditures by the government have totalled up to the end of 1943 the sum of $714,258,389 in government-owned industry and in assisting private industry. If the manufacturing and industrial situation in the maritime provinces is not improved during the war years by establishing industry with post-war prospects, I do not see that there is any hope in the years that are ahead. I say that it is the responsibility and the duty and the opportunity of the minister and the government to equalize industrial development in this country and establish and revive industries in the maritime provinces.
Unfortunately many of our products in the maritime provinces are basic commodities, such as iron and steel which sell for two or three cents a pound and are shipped elsewhere and manufactured into products costing as much as one or two dollars a pound. The same is true of lumber. It is largely produced and sold as a basic commodity. That applies also to the salt industry. Salt is sold as a basic commodity in our province at from three to four cents a pound, while it should be the basis of a great chemical industry. Our salt industry should be producing at the plant refined salt, soda ash and related compounds, salt cake (sodium sulphate), hydrochloric acid, caustic soda, chlorine, potash and other chemicals which are contained in our big deposits at Malagash. I hope that in these

War Appropriation-Supplies
appropriations we are now considering provision will be made for the development of a chemical industry based upon our salt resources.
Another big product in Nova Scotia is coal. Our coal is shipped at from four to five dollars per ton. Much of this might be converted and made into chemical products, valued up to a thousand dollars per ton. It appears to us that there might be established in Nova Scotia, on the basis of our raw materials, industries that would tend to equalize industrial activities in Canada and to some extent restore the position we held prior to and in the years following confederation. I hope that in the estimates now being considered provision is being made for development of our raw materials, which would be of benefit to Nova Scotia. I shall be glad to have from the minister a schedule of what he proposes under the very large appropriations that are now being considered by the committee.

In regard to the communication and signal programme, the minister reported to the committee, as appears at page 1696 of Hansard. May I ask what proportion if any of these large expenditures has been made in the maritime provinces? I will quote from the minister's statement at page 1696:
The value of our production in communications in 1940 was one million dollars, in 1942 60 million dollars; and in 1943 136 million dollars. The radio and communications industry is now operating at a level some eighteen times
greater than in 1939. We have orders on our books to the value of 400 million dollars, and we do not expect to reach peak production until the second quarter of 1944. To illustrate the diversity of the programme, I might point out that there are approximately 4,500 different items in current production by some fifty prime contractors and several hundred subcontractors.
And the next paragraph:
Some twenty major types of radar equipment have been developed for a variety of applications, ranging from one type for antiaircraft defence having 60,000 components, and 270 radio tubes, mounted in several large trucks, to small compact airborne units used for submarine detection at sea and target location on land.
What proportion of that large programme amounting to $400,000,000 has been undertaken in Nova Scotia? I do not want to be sectional; still I wish to point out to the committee and emphasize the fact that for many years we have not progressed industrially in that province. In manufacturing we have lost our position in relation to the rest of Canada. This is an opportunity such as we have never had since the decline of industry in that province, for the minister to do something for Nova Scotia. It is an opportunity that has come to no other government or minister to rectify the unfair conditions under which we have, existed in that province. Again I would inquire as to what proportion of this enormous development has taken place in Nova Scotia, a development involving in 1943 $136,000,060 and on our books, for the current year, the enormous sum of $400,000,000.

I do not know that I can
give the exact figures, but all that production is being obtained from existing manufacturing plants. The hon. member knows how many such plants there are in the maritime provinces and from that he can compute the probable output there. All suitable facilities of the country are being used for that purpose, including those in the maritime provinces, if any.

Following the hon. member for Cumberland, I think it is borne in upon the members of the committee that what should be undertaken without delay is a thorough survey of our resources in various parts of the country. The war has tended to concentrate industry more and more in a few places, and just as in Nova Scotia so in the western provinces, particularly Saskatchewan, we are going to feel after the war increasingly dependent on those parts of Canada where manufacturing industries have been established during the war. It seems to me that without delay there should be a thorough survey of

the resources of the country and we should endeavour to base, upon those resources, any further industrial development we undertake, on the principle of spreading them across the country instead of concentrating everything in one or two areas.
That was not what I rose primarily to say, however. This morning I placed some questions on the order paper and the Clerk of the House, quite properly I think, returned them to me because the questions involved the giving of some information. As we know, the rules of the house do not permit members giving information in the form of questions. But I wanted to find some information which comes under this particular item of the war appropriation, and so, instead of endeavouring to redraft the questions in a manner that might not be altogether satisfactory, I thought I would ask those questions now in the form in which I am going to put them.
I might say to the minister that I put the questions on the order paper because I did not want to prolong the discussion here. But I have had a number of inquiries lately as to whether or not there has been a change in the ownership of one of the companies with which we have been doing some business both in shipbuilding and in manufacturing of war equipment in Montreal. I refer particularly to the Canadian Vickers Limited. What is suggested to me is that a very considerable amount of stock of Canadian Vickers Limited, either a majority or a minority amount, I am not sure which, has passed into the control of a corporation known as Losanac Limited. In turn I am informed that Losanac Limited is a subsidiary of the Solvay Company of the United States; that this company is controlled by a corporation located in Basle, Switzerland, and that the holding company there is a company with a German name in which it is suggested to me there is a considerable amount of German capital even at the present time.
In my opinion it is in the public interest that the government of Canada should endeavour, if possible, to look into this situation to discover the facts, because Losanac is now the largest holder of preferred1 or common stock, I am told, of the International Nickel Company, and has substantial holdings in the Hollinger mine and other gold mines in the country, and also in the Dominion Steel and Coal Company and Asbestos Corporation. It it is, as I am informed, connected with the Solvay Company, that company had very large and important holdings in some fifteen or sixteen countries, including Great Britain, Japan, United States, Argentina, Brazil, Germany and others. In view of what we have learned during this war, particularly from
EMr, Coldwell.]
the investigations of the last twelve months or so in the United States regarding the associations of companies in all these countries with companies that engage in the provision of vital war material, it seems to me that the time has come to make every investigation that we can, to follow every lead that is given to us, in order to protect ourselves in future from the kind of thing that we have suffered from in the past. While this may not fall directly within the estimates of the minister, yet we are dealing with the war appropriation estimate as a whole. What I am about to say now will be said to save time in order to give the government the opportunity to look it up. In a recent official publication I came across a study made for the subcommittee on war mobilization of the committee on military affairs in the United States senate. It goes carefully into the associations of some of the corporations. The ones I refer to now are the I. G. Farben company and a British company known as Sterling Limited, of which some time before the war two of its directors were members of the I. G. Farben corporation. I want to read a statement in order that it may be looked up. The statement is as follows:
I G. Farben and Sterling also undertook to evade the tax laws of Canada. Under basic contracts, the profits of the Canadian Bayer Company were to be divided equally between Sterling and I.G. To reduce taxation, the payment to I.G. was misrepresented as a royalty, and charged as a cost of doing business. Remittances to I.G. were accompanied by the following statement:
You will note that the compensation paid to you has been deducted as an expense of the business. In the eyent that the Canadian government should ever determine that such payment to you is not properly deductible as an expense, and in consequence should require us to pay an additional tax, such tax will, of course, be charged against the total profits of the year in which such additional tax is required to be paid.
A similar practice was followed in the United States between 1920 and 1930. Eventually, however, it was disallowed by the income tax authorities and Sterling was required to pay half a million dollars in back taxes. Thereafter this method of accounting was discontinued in the United States but not in Canada.
I thought that later on when the appropriate minister is before us he might have looked into this situation. If we are able to collect some back taxes from this corporation, it would assist our war effort and our method of raising additional funds therefor. That is why I raise the tax suggestion at this time.
