I do not wish to delay passing of the minister's estimates for more than a moment. I should like to ask a question or two which I think will be of considerable interest to the public. My first question is with respect to a substance known as penicillin, a valuable therapeutic agent which is now being produced in Canada. It is being produced at the Connaught Laboratories in Toronto, I think, at the instigation of the minister himself. This discovery, perhaps one of the most important in recent years, was made by a British scientist. It is on a par with the discovery of the sulpha drugs, and has carried us one stage farther in our armamentarium which enables physicians to deal more effectually with certain heretofore frequently fatal diseases.
Will the minister tell the committee what arrangements he has made not only with the Connaught Laboratories at Toronto but with other laboratories or companies in Canada for the production of the substance known as penicillin? Second, when does he expect there will be a sufficient supply to meet the requirements of our armed forces; and third, when will a sufficient supply be made available for the civilian population?
Will the minister also give the committee an explanation of the crown company known as Defence Communications Limited? I believe it was set up by order in council, but I have not seen the order. Perhaps the minister would explain why this company was organized, what its purpose is, and if it will cease operations at the end of the war. Will he also make available to the committee a copy of the order in council?

With regard to the matter of penicillin, we have been acting under the guidance of the committee of the national research council whose responsibility it was to determine the requirements both of the armed services of Canada and of other uses, and to guide the department in the steps
taken to produce penicillin. On the advice of that committee we have established two sources of supply, one, the Connaught Laboratories in Toronto, and the other, a government-owned plant in Montreal operated for the government by Ayerst, McKenna and Harrison. We are now producing penicillin in a considerable quantity. I think we have fairly well taken care of the requirements of the armed forces from our own sources of supply. Production will be greater than was anticipated when the plants were organized. A committee in Washington, on which Canada has representation, is studying the supply situation in order to determine when penicillin can be released for other than military uses. No decision has been reached as yet, but it is my belief that within the next five or six months it will be possible to release penicillin for other than military uses. Does that answer the question?
Yes.

To answer the other question, Defence Communications is an outgrowth of the requirements of the armed services for communication systems in the eastern provinces. Each service was building its own communication system independently, and it was found that there was a great deal of overlapping. Finally the three services joined in requesting the Department of Munitions and Supply to undertake to provide communication services for all three branches of the armed forces. A crown company was formed called Defence Communications Limited, with which were filed the requirements of the armed services. Appropriations were made from the funds of the three armed services, and through that crown company a unified system of defence communications has been built. The work of the company is practically completed, and it is expected that the organization, which was a construction and not an operating company, can be dissolved within the next few months. I believe the operation of the company has resulted in a very considerable saving to the taxpayers, and I know the armed services are well pleased with the communication system that has ben worked out. The problem was not wholly one of construction; there was a certain amount of construction, but the problem was more particularly that of coordinating the services of private communication companies and combining with them the new construction that was necessary, so that the whole would give satisfactory service for defence purposes.

Before the minister leaves the question of penicillin, what is happening to Knox college in Toronto? Is it being rebuilt to manufacture penicillin?
War Appropriation-Supplies

It was taken over by Connaught Laboratories for the manufacture of penicillin, and for that purpose is being remodelled at government expense. It is just a building used by Connaught Laboratories for that purpose.
That is the sole use made of that building now?
Yes, as far as I know.
Has the minister any idea what the remodelling has cost?

It was three or four hundred thousand dollars; I do not remember the exact figure. I believe our investment with Connaught Laboratories for equipment and for remodelling the building is about $350,000.
Has the minister any idea of the expected output?
It is a unit with which I am not very familiar. I can tell my bon. friend there are a great many ciphers in front of the unit, but I am afraid I cannot go beyond that. It will be substantial.
Will the production in Toronto be greater than the production at the Ayerst plant in Montreal?
The intention was to have it about fifty-fifty.

I should like to revert for a moment to the question of coal, which was discussed this afternoon by the hon. member for Broadview. I should like to ask the minister two questions. First, what steps have been taken by the government to investigate the possibility of producing smokeless domestic coal from our bituminous coal by the low carbonization or other process, and are steps to be taken under any policy adopted or to be adopted by the government for further investigating the possibilities in this field? Second, what has been done, and what does the government propose, in regard to the production of oil from coal by the hydrogenation or any other similar process?
In connection with the first question I placed a question on the order paper last year; the answer was brought down on March 22, 1943, and appears at page 1418 of Hansard, as follows:
Studies of the more promising low temperature carbonization processes in operation in Europe and the United States were made by the mines branch of the Department of Mines during the period 1920 to 1930 when low temperature carbonization was a subject of particularly wide interest. Most Canadian coals were tested on a laboratory scale at the fuel research laboratories and the results of these tests were published in departmental reports.
	1
Subsequently arrangements were made to test Nova Scotia coal by one of the most promising processes developed up to that time and operating in South Wales. This test is reported in mines branch report No. 721, investigations of fuels and fuel testing 1929. The report concludes with the following statement:	"In
conclusion, it might be stated that it appears to the writers that in the case of the Sydney coal field there is an exceedingly good chance of converting bituminous coal into a domestic product, comparable to the existing fuels used for heating in central Canada, economically."
Then the answer goes on to explain that-
The hoped for development in Nova Scotia did not materialize and the anticipated expansion in low temperature carbonization generally did not take place.
As to the second question, I should like to direct the attention of the minister to information contained in a report made to the United States senate subcommittee on war mobilization, already referred to in this debate-

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I would point out to my hon. friend that there is no item in these estimates referring to the carbonization of coal. That would come under the Department of Mines and Resources, and though it is an interesting subject, it has nothing to do with the discussion being carried on to-day. I wonder if my hon. friend would mind waiting and bringing up his question when the estimates of the Minister of Mines and Resources are before the committee.

The minister made an important statement last Friday, and I should like to have it cleared up a little if I may. At page 1818 of Hansard for March 24, 1944, he is reported to have said:
During the last few months we have had sufficient steel for all reasonable purposes and the restrictions on use of steel in agricultural implements have been removed.
He also said that there was sufficient capacity for the manufacture of malleable castings in Canada to take care of the demand. Are we to understand from this statement that manufacturers in Canada now may obtain sufficient steel to take care of the demand for new agricultural implements, particularly in the west? During what we speak of as the depression years the machinery on the farms were not kept in repair; then the war came along, and much of the machinery is practically worn out. There is quite a demand now for new machines, and they are very difficult to get. Before I left home in January I had some experience with the permits required by the prices board in order to purchase new machines, but if this statement means that the manufacturers will be

IFar Appropriation-Supplies
allowed sufficient steel to take care of the demand I think it will be a splendid thing, particularly in view of the man-power situation. In the last two years particularly the use of power equipment in the production of grain has considerably increased, and I hope the equipment will be forthcoming to enable this development to continue. It would be a splendid thing also if enough repair parts could be supplied to take care of the requirements in that line.
While I am on my feet I should like to say a word or two with respect to the production of alcohol from grain. There has been a good deal of discussion in that connection, and we know what is happening in the United States.
I hope the minister will keep in mind the possibility of permitting some industries to be established in the west, right where the grain is produced, to provide facilities for the production of alcohol from grain to be used in the manufacture of synthetic rubber. I may say also that with the power we will have when the men come back from overseas, and the increased man-power which will be available to operate power equipment, it will be possible to produce grain cheaper than it is being produced to-day. It is not fair to compare the price of grain to-day, when we are considering the cost of producing alcohol from grain, with what the condition will be after the war, because we will be producing grain much cheaper than it is being produced to-day. The committee would be surprised if I were to state the price at which one of my constituents produced 18,000 bushels of wheat last year. He has a record of it. I would not like to say exactly what he produced it for, because it might cause the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Trade and Commerce to refrain from increasing the price, as we would like to see it to-day.
This afternoon, the hon. member for Macdonald referred to the lumber question. Certainly the independent dealers have not been getting as much as they would like. But the lumber they are getting, that which is being distributed in the central part of Saskatchewan, is not of the quality it should be. The hon. member for Melfort discussed that question this afternoon. Some action could be taken by those who are in control of the lumber supply to see that the people in the southern part of Saskatchewan get a better quality of lumber. It is available. Of course I can appreciate the fact that for the export market the large dealers have to have a high grade of lumber. I believe, however, that if a check-up were made on those producing lumber in the northern part of the province, a better quality could be produced and could be made available to the interior.
I would ask the minister to make a statement with respect to the supply of steel to the implement companies manufacturing in Canada. Do we understand from his statement that there will be a more liberal distribution of implements available for production in western Canada?
In 1939 the steel used by implement companies amounted to 30,150 tons. For 1944-45 we have released 81,750 tons of steel to the implement companies, which is an increase of 271 [DOT] 1 per cent.

In the report of subcommittee No. 4 of the war expenditures committee, which appears in Votes and Proceedings for Wednesday, January 26, 1944, there are set out certain shortages which still exist and which retard the production of ample quantities of farm implements. That report shows shortages of malleable castings, ball and roller bearings, seasoned fir and oak required for the production of certain types of farm machinery, and experienced man-power.
I am quite sure that the minister has given some consideration to the recommendations of this committee. I never could quite understand why this committee in its deliberations and in the taking of evidence should have been sitting behind closed doors, as was the case with some of the other committees. That is my view, after looking over the report. I cannot see that much comfort could be given to the enemy by anything that would be discussed so far as farm implements were concerned.
That brings me to this one point: Was it the suggestion of the minister or of the government that rubber production, or synthetic rubber production, particularly the operations of Polymer in Sarnia, should be submitted to the war expenditures committee at this time for consideration? I understand that one of those subcommittees is about to deal with Polymer and synthetic rubber.

I have never at any time made any such suggestion, and I think it is a very improper suggestion to say that I have. These committees are investigating my department. They investigate where they like and as they like. It certainly would be improper for me to send them on a wild goose chase, or otherwise. I do not like the suggestion.

The minister is picking up every kind of question that is directed to him, as a suggestion. If he will go over my remarks carefully he will find that I did not even hint that he had made any such suggestion. I only asked him at whose suggestion it was made, and whether he had made it. Because it would seem to me that with the Polymer plant only
War Appropriation-Supplies

starting, and with synthetic production getting under way, there are very many other things at which the war expenditures committees might more properly be employing their talents, and this was one of the things which might perhaps be left over. I never have heard any serious complaint about synthetic rubber production or about the set-up of Polymer- except in some quarters, with respect to the whole mafter of government crown companies, which is a general subject, or might be described as a general line of policy which some take. I am glad to hear that it was not the minister who was sending the committee on an investigation of that kind. Even if it were necessary to have this particular matter investigated prior to other matters, it did not seem to me that there was much reason for investigating this plant.

I am one member of the committee which is going to visit the synthetic rubber plant. I think the suggestion was made -because I was there when it was made- that the product was so good and the output so wonderful that the committee should visit the plant merely in order to see it, not to investigate the output or what was being done.

That just raises the whole question. I do not know whether this means now that the war expenditures committee is going on a lot of joy rides so far as this whole question is concerned, that is the way the hon. member indicates it. If this is one of those wonderful plants, I know of no reason why the war expenditures committee, which might be putting its time to better use, I think, need to be taking a trip of that kind at the country's expense.

A statement of that kind is very much uncalled for. I have been a member of the committee for three years, and I have never had any joy trip yet. But if I took a trip, or took it upon myself at any time to visit a plant, just because I was anxious to get information and see how the work was done,
I would resent its being called a joy ride. I say it is most uncalled for to refer to it as a joy ride. Personally I want to see what is deing done.

So far as a joy ride is concerned, the hon. member himself was the one who gave the description which led me so to designate it. I was not suggesting that the hon. member was taking a joy ride because of the work he had to do on the committee. It does not reflect upon him. But if the facts are as he has indicated, that we are going to some of our best plants to see what is going 
on, then surely that is carrying the work of the war expenditures committee much farther than was intended.

It is going too far to say that the war expenditures committee is to have no Opportunity to see what is being done. I believe it would pay you to go and see it. You do not seem anxious to go to see what is being done.

I suggest that this debate is entirely out of order. I cannot see the impropriety of the war expenditures committee, set up to protect the taxpayers of Canada, looking into the expenditure of $45,000,000 of the taxpayer's money. I think that is a very proper excursion.

I pointed out that there was a variation between the figures of the war expenditures committee and those of the minister. If we could have it clearly stated by the minister that there is no shortage of steel or of other raw materials going into the manufacture of farm implements, then when we come to the Minister of Labour and national selective service and the wartime prices and trade board we may be able to get to the root of this matter. A greater production of farm implements is sadly needed at the present time. We have been led to believe that the chief difficulty is the shortage of steel and raw materials. The farmer has been willing to labour under almost any disadvantage if steel and raw materials are not available, but more labour-saving implements should be made available as soon as possible. If these materials are available, then we can take up the matter when we are dealing with the other departments.

I have just given the figures.
I have nothing to do with the production of farm implements, other than to release certain strategic materials, one of which is steel. This year we have allocated 271-1 per cent as compared with what was used in 1939, which was a fairly good year. That is quite a bit of steel, and I dare say that if more is needed we shall be able to allocate more.
More labour would help production.
I do not know about labour.

When we made our inquiry into the production of farm implements we received the assurance of the steel controller that he would see to it that the implement producers received sufficient steel to carry on their programmes. But there is a definite shortage of ball bearings and malleable castings. Ball bearings are not produced in Canada, and I know that the plant at home

War Appropriation-Supplies
has had extreme difficulty in obtaining this product as well as malleable castings. We had the officials before us; we endeavoured to point out as best we could the situation in connection with the supply of both these products, and we had their assurance that they would give every consideration to seeing that the implement producers obtained supplies.
I must say that we had the best of cooperation from all officials who appeared before the committee. We carried out an inquiry which I think was very useful. We presented the situation from the manufacturers' viewpoint and we received representations from farmers and from the federation of agriculture. I have spent a good deal of my life in this business and I think I know something about it'. I believe I know what the implement manufacturers are up against in getting supplies of certain items. That is one reason why we made the recommendations we did. Because of the greatly increased use of tractors and other implements of the kind, the time has come when Canadian manufacturers should see that more of these items are produced in Canada. I hope that the recommendations we made will have some effect.

I placed most of the names of those officials on the record when I was speaking previously. Is the hon. member of the opinion that ball bearings and malleable castings will be produced in Canada in the near future?

Malleable castings are
made in Canada at the present time, but they are in short supply both here and in the United States. We felt that it would be in the interests of the farm producers to recommend that a subsidy be paid in connection with the production of malleable castings. We know there is a tremendous shortage of labour and if our farmers are going to produce what we want them to produce they must have these implements and labour saving devices. Every official before us intimated that he would cooperate to the fullest extent.
Brantford roofing.

That would be the very best you could possibly put on a farm building if you wanted roofing of that kind. The trouble is that where you have a barn with open siding it is not as satisfactory as the steel roof. The steel roof will stand higher winds. I know of many buildings that need roofs badly. We are producing many products which must be kept under cover, and serious consideration should be given to this phase of the matter. I have often wondered why more pressure has not been brought to bear upon the minister in connection with this matter.
Another matter was brought to the attention of the committee on Tuesday, March 21, by the hon. member for Lake Centre. He wanted to know what disposition would be made by the government of the temporary buildings which had been built for war purposes. Then he said, as reported at page 1716 of Hansard:
I would point out that I have not yet received an answer to the question as to whether or not it is the intention of this government to operate any industries after the war in opposition to private enterprise.
I consider that that question should not go unanswered. I think the people of Canada are anxious to know which way we are drifting. H have no hesitation in stating where I stand. I take the position that we must do everything possible to protect the principle of free enterprise in the main. Only where free enterprise cannot function in the best interests
War Appropriation-Supplies

of humanity should the government lend its support. I know where the people whom I represent stand on the principle of free enterprise. They are in favour of maintaining this principle which has brought Canada to the high standard of living now enjoyed by our people. True, there must be corrections made from time to time, and I have every reason to believe that we can make those corrections. But I think the minister would be wise in making a declaration of policy, particularly since he has shown himself a master of organized enterprise in accomplishing what he has accomplished in this war. It has been largely done under the policy of free enterprise. Perhaps the fact that Canada's contribution is the greatest per capita of any of the united nations is because in no other country has free enterprise had full sway as it has in Canada. Furthermore, what we have accomplished has been done at far less expense than what has been accomplished in other countries. In spite of our magnificent effort we have kept the per capita debt of our people down; it is much less than the per capita debt of our neighbours to the south and of Australia, New Zealand and almost any other country. That in itself is a credit to the policy of free enterprise under which we have worked and a tribute to the minister in organizing industry in Canada. I have always stood for the principle of free enterprise, and L hope that we shall be able to maintain it in this dominion.
I noticed that the hon. member for Lake Centre, when he asked the minister to make a statement of policy, seemed to have qualms as to the position of his own party on free enterprise. I noticed that the Globe and Mail in November last reported speeches in which the Hon. George Drew and his minister of agriculture stated that it was the intention of the Progressive Conservative party in Ontario to go in for making refrigerators, bathtubs and such like, at cost, for the benefit of the farmers. So that we know which way they are going.
Are you objecting to that?
You told us about bathtubs in the first speech you made in this house.
I take issue with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle hecause I did not. I am afraid he, too, must be suffering from qualms of conscience to bring that up.
You have not answered my question yet.
One at a time.
Are you objecting to the proposal of lower cost of refrigeration and bathtubs for the farmers?
I did not say that.
I think you are wise to-keep away from it.

The hon. member has not shown too much wisdom himself, so that I do not think he needs to give advice, much as I respect him and enjoy his friendship. But he does blow a fuse quite often in his remarks.
I was going on to say that the Globe and Mail reported the Hon. T. L. Kennedy, minister of agriculture in the Ontario government, as having said:
It is my idea that the government would finance the manufacture of these-[DOT]
That is refrigerators.
-and sell them to the farmers at actual cost price.	.
Is that what you are objecting to?
That is not the point. I am speaking of the principle involved.
Are you objecting to the principle?

I would object because I do not think the government can manufacture and sell them at cost as well as private enterprise. I want the farmers to get the best deal possible and I believe it is better to let them get these things through private enterprise. The Retail Merchants' Association was concerned over this proposal of the Ontario government and considerable correspondence passed between them and the minister of agriculture in the Ontario government about it. What I am drawing attention to is that we now have the Progressive Conservative party declaring itself on the principle of going into the manufacture of articles which private enterprise has made a fairly good job of manufacturing in the past. We now know where the Progressive Conservative party stands. We also know where our Cooperative Commonwealth Federation friends stand, because they have declared themselves definitely for the nationalization of industry.
What item are we on, Mr. Chairman? How long have we to put up with this?

I do not take up very much of the time of this chamber. As a quiet member, maybe I do a little more thinking than some other hon. members, and these are some of the matters I have been thinking about. I

War Appropriation-Supplies
thought it wise to draw to the attention of the committee the road we are travelling. All we can judge a party by is the things it does, not what its members talk about. I was saying that under the principle of free enterprise we have made a magnificent effort in this war. On the other hand, if the Progressive Conservatives have declared themselves for the nationalization of the refrigeration and bathtub industry and such like-
Haldimand-Norfolk, the county next to yours, seemed to like it.
I am not so sure. I would not take too much glory to myself over that. One sparrow does not make a summer by any means.
Did a sparrow ever?

The fact of the matter is, I think, that the minister should not let this opportunity pass to make a statement of his viewpoint on the principle of free enterprise. Ours has been a magnificent accomplishment to the extent of around live billion dollars under -more or less of a mixed policy.
I believe we have a right, to know what the future has in store for us, and I hope we shall hear from the minister.

On
March 21 I asked the minister for the total amount of purchases for the United States that had been made by the United States purchasing branch of his department.
I told my hon. friend that I did not care to give that figure.
That problem is not in my department. It comes under the administrator of services, which is under the wartime prices and trade board.
Does it not come under transit control?
Not trucks.

I have another item. This is from the Department of Munitions and Supply, being one of its releases in regard to construction and alteration of plants. They have jumped the value from $2,500 to $5,000. Up to $5,000 a permit
is not needed. The same change applies to the installation of equipment in plants. What I want to get at is this. There is an order, which I believe is 284, which does not allow a plant to be extended with new machinery being put in. You cannot put new machinery in a new space. Does this do away with that order?

No. If it is all one project it should be so named. If the project extends the plant and installs machinery in the extension, and should it cost more than $5,000, a permit is needed. On the other hand, if it is simply a question of installing machinery in an existing plant, that machinery can be installed up to $5,000 without a permit being required. But each must be a complete transaction.

Yes; but suppose a firm own a building next to them. They could not take a machine from the building in which that machine is already installed and put it into the other building. Here you are extending the plant; you are allowing them to extend the plant and put in new machinery.
The safest thing for my hon. friend's friends to do is to apply for a permit. Permits are not hard to get.

This firm applied before the order came out and they were refused permission to put one of their machines into another building which they owned. I want to find out whether this order that has now come out cancels the controls that formerly obtained.
It amends the control order. That is the order my hon. friend has been referring to, but I cannot give interpretations of even' order put out.
Neither can the manufacturers, and that is the trouble. Sometimes they are held up for months, while the firm is anxious to go ahead and manufacture, in most cases munitions.

A few days ago I asked the minister about the programme of subcontracting machine shops in mining companies in Canada. They were doing rather extensive retooling work. Was the programme successful or was it gone into?

Yes, the programme was very successful. We have had a great many ship components made by machine shops of the mining industry as well as by machine shops of the pulp and paper industry. That capacity not only has meant a considerable saving in the installation of new machine tools but has

War Appropriation-Supplies

distributed the work where the man-power was available and has been helpful in the whole programme.
Is it still going on?
Yes.

I should like to secure information in connection with the availability of man-power. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) yesterday referred to the need of combing industry in order to secure the necessary men for the armed forces during the months to come. The first question I want to ask in that regard is this: Is there to-day, or has there been within the past three months, any shortage of man-power in any of the key industries under the minister's control? If so, in what industries and to what extent is there or has there been a shortage?

We always have shortages in certain industries. Shortages vary from time to time. In the last two or three months the most acute shortages have been in the malleable casting industry and in the motor vehicle industry. As far as I know, the motor vehicle industry has never had all the men that could be used. There are other industries in which there are shortages from time to time. Certain shortages develop and are corrected, but the main shortages of the past three months have been in the two that I have mentioned. Of course, in lumber we could always use more men than were available. The cut of lumber is proportionate to the number of men engaged in the industry, and if we had twice as many men we could perhaps cut twice as much lumber. There is a demand at home and abroad for all the lumber that can be cut. In base metals the situation was acute but has been largely straightened out. The man-power situation is not bad in the base metal mines; the shortages are in the rougher and heavier jobs.
What is the amount of shortage from month to month?
I cannot say; the Minister of Labour could tell the hon. member that.
Well, the minister is in charge of the department and he was able to give information to the press as to the shortage a few months ago.
What did I say?

In the Toronto
Star, the minister is reported as having stated on December 2, 1943:
There is a shortage of 55,000 male workers and 16,000 female workers in the highest priority war industries alone.

These figures apparently were available to the minister then. He must have figures showing the situation from month to month in regard to man-power. The allocation of man-power naturally falls on the shoulders of the Minister of Labour. The responsibility for mobilization is his. The question I am asking the Minister of Munitions and Supply is this. Is there a shortage to-day of male and female workers in the war industries? If so, what is the latest available figure on such shortage?

Does my hon. friend wish me to give him the statistics of the Department of Labour? He can get those from the Department of Labour. It happens that I have them, but I do not know why I should give them to him.
If the minister has the information, surely he has no objection to giving it.

They are given to us as confidential; I do not know how confidential. However, I will give the figures. On March 10, 1944, unfilled vacancies in A priority industries were 30,411; in B priority industries, 24,408; in C priority industries, 6,115; in D priority industries, 10,158. The total of priority labour requirements was 71,092.
I do not know whether this information can be given, but is the minister in a position to advise what is the nature of A, B, C, and D priorities? What industries fall under them?
That is confidential.

Well, I will not press that because I can understand that there might be such a situation. The minister is reported to have stated recently that certain single-purpose plants have been closed down and in particular that one or more explosive factories have been changed into fertilizer factories. Have any explosive factories been closed down; if so, where? Which ones have been changed into fertilizer factories? I believe this is the first example of a transition from war-time to peace-time production.

The only plant manufacturing explosives that has been closed down .that I know of is the plant at Nobel. We had three plants manufacturing propellants and explosives, one at Winnipeg, one at Nobel and one at de Salaberry. The operation at the Nobel plant was of a type that could best be spared. It was a question of operating each of them at half capacity or closing one and operating the other two at a rate of capacity that would mean efficient production. It was therefore decided to close down

War Appropriation-Supplies
the Nobel plant. The other plants to which my hon. friend refers are plants manufacturing ammonia for explosives. One plant is at Calgary. It is government-owned, and the other is at Welland, also government-owned. The full production of ammonia from those plants was not required for explosives. All surplus ammonia is now being used in making ammonia nitrate by a process worked out in the plants themselves. The ammonia nitrate is found to make a very good fertilizer. The two elements required in the synthetic fertilizer are ammonia and nitrate. The product of these plants has a wide sale at attractive prices.
The plant at Calgary is not a government plant?
Oh, yes.

Mr. Chairman the scandals and the shameful favouritism which have been brought to light in war industries are such as to make the government conscious of the distressing deficiencies of the national selective service. An investigation should be held at once by a royal commission about employment at the Bouchard plant. The investigation should also bear upon the administration of the Sainte Therese local office of the national selective service. The government should not elude their responsibility by arguing that private companies are involved. The government give those companies financial assistance running into hundreds of millions of dollars. Let the government insist on calling them to account, and the people will be satisfied. Since we are fighting for the triumph of justice and right, unfairness should not be rampant as regards employment in war industries, nor should it prevail in other fields.

Would the parliamentary assistant to the minister give us some indication with regard to the supply of tinplate for making cans for canning vegetables? Is there a shortage and what will the situation be this year?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: I presume what the hon. member for Peterborough West is asking about is galvanized plate.
No; tinplate for canning fruit.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Munitions and Supply
speechtext: The position is that tinplate is in short supply all across the country and there is very little hope of its being released.

When I visited Deep Brook training camp and some of the other training camps I noticed that the
canned milk which was supplied to the men was given to them in quart tins, and in one place just before the meal hour they dumped the milk into jugs. There must have been hundreds and hundreds of these quart cans. Would anything be saved if that milk were given to them in gallon cans? I think a lot of tinplate would be saved if the milk were put in gallon cans.

I do not know whether the minister has made any statement in connection with the importation of domestic coal into Ontario for the coming winter and what the situation is to be. What is the prospect for obtaining coal in large cities like Toronto? I think the citizens of Toronto used a great deal less coal last year than they would otherwise have used, and that was owing to the request that was made. Would the minister make a statement as to what the prospects are?

The coal requirements of Ontario are necessarily imported from the United States. Last year we were able to obtain sufficient bituminous coal for oui requirements. In the matter of anthracite we obtained the same proportion of our total requirements as was issued to the citizens of the United States. There was a shortage. I think actually we received about three-quarters of our requirements. I presume that the United States will treat us as one of their own in the matter of coal in future as they did this year. If there is a shortage in the United States we will expect to share that shortage. Whether there will be a shortage or not I cannot say. I referred to the matter when I made my statement in the house and I urged users of domestic coal, particularly in the central Canada area, to be as economical as possible with their coal.

With regard to coal, I have a letter here from one of the largest dealers in anthracite. It is addressed to one of his dealers and reads in part as follows:
The new programme readjusts each dealer's tonnage for the current season to approximately eighty-two per cent of his last year's shipments. Until about December 15 . . . anthracite went forward on the basis of a ninety per cent programme. . . .
That would be eighty-two per cent of what they received last year, which was only ninety per cent. The complaint in the city of Peterborough is that some of the coal they are getting there now is unfit to burn. We have practically no anthracite in Peterborough. The burning of soft coal means that at the end of the season practically all homes will have to be
War Appropriation-Supplies

redecorated, because the soft coal makes a mess of the home. They are very anxious to get some of the Alberta coal.

For many years past the government have been paying a subsidy on coal produced at the Comox mine in Cumberland, British Columbia, and possibly also in Nanaimo. That has nothing to do with war services. I should like to ask the minister if they are receiving or if they will receive any subsidy under the war measures that he is handling, and whether it would be affected in any way by the orders in council to which he referred yesterday? I refer to the orders in council which make changes in the war subsidies.

There was no provision for subsidies in the statement I made in the last day or two. It covered only the mainland and prairie mines. I am not sure of the position of the British Columbia mines, but I shall be glad to get the information from the . coal emergency board and advise my hon. friend.

In connection with plants manufacturing munitions of war, and especially in connection with subcontractors, when it is anticipated that some particular article may not be needed in the near future does the department advise the contractor or subcontractor a reasonable length of time ahead, so that the necessary adjustments may be made? As the minister knows, from time to time there have been rumours as to lay-offs at the Toronto Shipbuilding Company, and I understand the mayor of Toronto has taken up the matter with the minister. What is the position there now? What is the backlog of orders? How long will the Toronto Ship-buildirig Company be in full operation? Is this advance information, which I think is important, given to the plants concerned, in order that they may adjust their processes accordingly?

When we are notified of a programme change the plant that is interested in that programme is advised immediately; and if a lay-off is contemplated in the near future, selective service is advised at the same time. The hon. gentleman asked about the backlog of orders for the Toronto Shipbuilding Company. Unless there are further cancellations, the Toronto Shipbuilding Company has all the work it can do this season.

The minister said that his department notified selective service. In order that the organization within the plant may be kept together instead of having

the men go elsewhere to work, is any endeavour made by the department to substitute the manufacture of some other article which may be in short supply?

My hon. friend was referring to the Toronto Shipbuilding Company. There is no problem of substitution in that case; the yard is busy at the work for which it was organized. Any lay-offs in the past resulted from the fact that the yard was overstaffed, and in the reorganization of the management the staff was brought down to a normal operating level. There is no shortage of work there.

I could have mentioned several other plants. For instance, what about the Sutton Horsley plant, where the staff has been reduced by about fifty per cent? The minister stated that this plant had been engaged in the manufacture of instruments for training planes. Is there any reason why it could not have been given other orders instead of laying off those employees? I was not referring particularly to the Toronto Shipbuilding Company; I was using that just as an example. While I am on my feet, the minister said he did not think the great lakes yards would be able to build freighters because of the tonnage and draught.
I did not say anything of the kind.

Last evening, in answer to a question I asked, the minister said, as reported at page 1896 of Hansard:
The type of boat which can be built on the lakes is restricted, either to tonnage for the great lakes, or to tonnage which can pass through the St. Lawrence canals.
The tonnage really does not affect it; the lake boats are of all sizes, some of them quite large. I was wondering whether in future these yards would be capable of manufacturing lake freighters economically.
The lake yards have built all the lake freighters there are; they are still at least as efficient as ever they were, and I think they will continue to build the lake freighters.
They have not built them all.
Oh, yes.

I should like to ask a supplementary question, in regard to the manufacture of tools and small parts by some of the mining plants throughout Canada. At the beginning of the war the mining company at Inverness, which has an efficient

TFar Appropriation-Supplies
machine shop, made application for work of this kind. I understand that the plant was investigated, but no contracts have been offered. I wonder if the investigation disclosed that this work could not be done economically or satisfactorily, or that the requirements could not be met. Could the minister give some information as to why this plant was not given any contracts?
Of course there are thousands of subcontracts, but I shall be glad to look up the report on that plant and advise my hon. friend later on.
The minister told us what had been done in connection with coal. Does he know what the prospects are for the future?

No. Future prospects in connection with coal for the Toronto area are beyond my control; we are dependent upon the United States for that coal. We shall do our very best to get the largest possible supply that can be made available.

The distribution of the coal and the quantities allotted to individuals come under the control of the minister, and people wish to know the prospects of getting coal from the United States. Is the supply going to be long or short? People want to make their arrangements as early as possible.

A few moments ago the parliamentary assistant partly explained the situation in regard to tinplate. Last year there was a considerable shortage in the production of canned vegetables in particular. Was there any carryover of tinplate or cans last year? Did I understand the parliamentary assistant to say that tinplate was still in very short supply and there was little chance of an increase in the supply this year?

This year the government is urging greater production, and is increasing the subsidy oil some of these commodities. Will the minister explain the present position respecting the iron mine at Steep Rock. What progress has been made; what money has been spent, and what are the commitments?

War Appropriation-Supplies

The mine at Steep Rock has nothing to do with these estimates. It is a project brought before the cabinet as a whole by the Canadian National Railways. One difficulty about opening up the mine was that existing freight rates were not competitive with freight rates from the Mesabi range to Duluth. Government assistance was given to equalize freight rates for a period. The rate was equalized for the movement of the first 5,000,000 tons, and by assistance to the extent of twenty cents a ton for that movement. In addition, the government undertook to finance for the railways an ore dock at the head of the lakes to permit ore to be transferred from rail to boat.
What progress has been made?

I know very little more than my hon. friend; all I know is what I have read in the press. I understand, however, that the dewatering process is well advanced. In the last statement I saw, it was predicted that ore would be produced from the mine in August.
In August of this year?
Yes.

I have one other question, respecting subsidies paid on coal. As I understand it, when wages were raised last fall a subsidy was paid on coal imported from the United States which, of course, is used largely in central Canada. The price to the consumer remained what it had been before the increase in wages. But in the west the price of coal was allowed to go up. Will the minister explain why that was done, and whether that is still the position? It would seem to have been an unfair move, so far as the western consumer is concerned. However, there may have been some reason for that action.

The government is subsidizing practically all domestic coal production in the west to-day. I have read in this house the revised subsidies, some of which are substantial. They were built up in order to keep uneconomical mines in operation during a period of great scarcity. I read in the house two or three days ago a revised schedule of subsidies which provide for subsidies varying from sixty-five cents down to fifteen cents a ton. These arose out of increases in the cost of living bonus and in wages, prior to the wage increase to wffiich the hon. member has referred, which increases were beyond the capacity of the mines to meet. The operators could not stand the increased cost of production, and to keep the mines in operation the government paid a subsidy. It was felt that the government could not be put in a
rMr. Green.]
position of being forced to subsidize every time a mine found it necessary to increase wages. When the increase came last summer it was pointed out that if more wages were necessary an increase in the price of the product would also be necessary. Then the hon. member referred to a bonus on imported coal in central Canada.
The point I have made is that the price to the consumer was raised in the west, but not in the east.

There was no similar situation in the east. Bituminous coal brought into the central provinces from the United States is not bonused. It is bought by dealers at the going rates, and is resold to the public without any bonus. On anthracite there is a small subsidy.
Is a subsidy paid on it.

No, not on bituminous; but there is a small subsidy on anthracite, amounting to about twenty or twenty-five cents a ton. I cannot tell my hon. friend just how it arises. I think there was at the source of origin an increased cost, which, it was felt, could not be passed on to the producer at the time. The subsidy amounts to something less than twenty-five cents a ton-possibly twenty cents a ton. Certainly it is not more than twenty-five cents. So that the subsidy paid in the east, even on anthracite, is less than the subsidy paid in the west or in the mari times.
The trouble was that the price went up in the west and it did not go up in the east.

Yes, but when a gun is put
to our heads in a time of great emergency, sometimes we have to take what comes. The government cannot be placed in the position of subsidizing a product every time it becomes necessary to raise wages.
What was the basis for subsidizing in the east?
The same basis as for subsidizing in the west. We subsidize western coal to-day, anywhere from fifteen to sixty-five cents a ton.
The basis for subsidizing soft coal in the east was not the same, because stoker coal has gone up from about $7 or $8 a ton before the war to a present price of $11.

It is not subsidized.

War Appropriation-Supplies
And the same with steam coal?
It is not subsidized, either.
The public have to pay the extra cost; that is the answer. I do not quite understand why eastern coal, under the same circumstances, should not have been subsidized.
Eastern coal is subsidized.
Eastern coal is?
Maritime coal, yes.

I do not mean that.
I mean central coal. Our people in the central provinces have to pay for it. It is a matter of keeping the cost of living down; that is the idea of the subsidy. It is a serious problem, especially in the city of Toronto where rentals are frozen. ,The Toronto Housing Company, a philanthropic organization with which I am connected, cannot get more rentals, and we are faced with $5,000 or $6,000 a year more than we used to pay in our outlay for coal. The east and the west are subsidized, but we in the central provinces are not. That does not seem to be a position of equality.

Under this item I should like to refer to the announcement that the minister made yesterday with respect to the revised subsidy policy affecting the western domestic coal fields. I imagine that the outline he gave of subsidies is over and above the regular subsidies that are given for the movement of coal in Canada.

Yes.
War Appropriation-Supplies

I am very happy to hear the minister say that, because I believe that in war time we have discovered that certain subsidies have to be paid in connection with the coal mining industry. With the announcement of these subsidies the minister also stated that the government will appoint a royal commission charged with the duty of studying all aspects of the production and distribution of coal in Canada and to report to the government with recommendations for such alterations of the pre-war coal policy as its findings may indicate to be necessary or desirable.
I have no objection to another coal commission being appointed to go into the various aspects of the coal mining industry, but I would point out that, as the minister is well aware, this is not the first commission that will have been appointed for work of this kind. If we look back over the history of the coal mining industry in Canada we shall discover that a good many coal commissions have been set up, and I cannot quite understand why it should be necessary now to set up another one. I am not opposing it, but I know that in the past commissions have studied every possible aspect of the coal mining industry. They have investigated1 and studied the matter of freight rates, the matter of subventions on coal, the matter of the various kinds and types of coal, and I believe the national research council has done considerable work along similar lines. I am tempted, therefore, to ask what action governments of the past have really taken as a result of these various commissions on coal.
Some action may have been taken, particularly with reference to subventions, but I suggest that there is no use in appointing commissions if the government is not going to be sincere in accepting their findings and bringing about, on the basis of those findings, such legislation as will benefit the coal mining industry and the consumers of coal, meaning, of course, everybody.
I said a moment ago that I was not going to oppose the setting up of another commission; but I cannot help feeling that, coming at this time as it does, this is nothing more or less than a political move on the part of the government in order to give the people of Canada the impression that it is going to do something in connection with the coal mining industry. I consider that that is all it is, because if the government wanted to do something it could take the findings of commissions in days gone by and upon those findings bring about a national coal policy.
That is something that Canada has never had. Not only have commissions worked oh these matters in the past, but the coal mining industry itself has worked hard to put the
TMr. Howe.]
industry over in Canada. I recall not so many years ago, since I became a member of parliament, that coal miners and coal operators in various sections of Alberta got together-and that is something, when operators and miners get together on a project-and attempted to form an organization for the purpose of securing markets for Alberta coal.
That was an admirable thing and they tried their best; but the coal situation in Canada being what it was, with various, shall I say, combines, their efforts amounted to very little. The only solution for the coal mining problem is that Canada should have Canadian markets for Canadian coal, notwithstanding anything that anyone might have said with reference to the type of coal that is mined in this country. I am confident that until Canada is reserved as the market for coal mined in Canada the national coal problem will not be solved.
I wish to ask the minister this question: In what way has the situation changed in Canada to necessitate the appointment of another commission? Is the coal situation any different from what it was before the war started? I do not believe it is. If the minister can enlighten us on it, well and good, but I do not think the situation has changed one bit. The war has done something to increase markets for Canadian coal because of the very high productive capacity of Canadian industry at this time; but as far as consumption of coal and employment in coal mines in Canada are concerned, would the minister tell us in what way the situation has changed; what the changes are, and whether the position is any different now from what it was in pre-war days? If he can tell us of the change, then we shall recognize the need for another commission. If he cannot, why not take the findings of past commissions and work on them? Once again I say, unless he can explain that to the committee I regard the setting up of this new commission as a political move to make the people of Canada feel that something is to be done in order to let them down as they have been let down many times before; and we shall still find the coal mining industry trying to get along on crutches. That is the position. I should like the minister to answer that question for us.

The coal situation has changed materially in the course of the war. The principal change has been in the greatly increased cost of producing coal, which increased cost is general in our Canadian mines. The loss of skilled miners has had an effect, and other factors have entered into the situation, so that the markets which can be reached on a competitive basis are quite different to-day from the competitive position of before the

War Appropriation-Supplies
war. Before the war the mines in the maritime provinces shipped coal as far west as Toronto, Sudbury and the lake St. John area. The western limit for maritime coal to-day is about Riviere du Loup; and the maritime mines are hard put to supply the demands of their own provinces.
The western mines have been handicapped, not only by the increased cost of the product at the pit-head, but also by shortages of transportation, owing to the burden that has been put on the railways to move other high priority commodities. To keep the mines going to meet unusually heavy demands, a system of subsidies has been built up, on a more or less haphazard basis. We have been in the position of not wishing to allow any producing mine to close down, and, as costs have risen, we have tried to keep the mine open by paying whatever subsidy has been required. The recent mild winter has allowed us a breathing space to review the situation, and we are revising subsidies that are obviously out of line. We are studying subsidies for other cases which require considerable accounting and auditing, and further revisions of subsidies in those areas will be made. But having in mind the changes in marketing conditions, the change in economic areas for marketing, and the changes in the cost of production, the government believes that a commission is needed now more urgently than at any time in the past. I have every confidence that a commission that can study every aspect of the production and marketing of coal in Canada will bring down a report which will be helpful to the government in formulating a new coal policy for Canada.
While I am on my feet I shall give the hon. member for Comox-Alberni an answer to the question he asked. The new subsidy arrangement does not apply to mines on Vancouver island. Canadian Collieries on Vancouver island is on the old form of subsidy, which will not be changed until the present audit, which is now proceeding, is completed.

The
minister spoke of assistance by way of subsidies being given to coal mines that are finding it difficult to operate. Does he mean that the assistance was given to them by allowing them to increase the price of coal? Is that what he refers to, or is it a direct subsidy to the mine? The government allowed an increase in price to some of the mines that were finding it difficult to operate. Is that what the minister meant when he spoke of a subsidy?
We have given considerable direct assistance to the mines either by way of subsidy, or by way of new equipment for expanding production.
That was in addition to allowing them to increase their price?

The increase in price resulted from one incident, namely, a strike at a critical time. The result of that was an increase in wages. That is compensated for by an increase in the price of the product being permitted.
What is the amount of the subsidy paid on imported coal?

I have been over that at least five times to-day, but I shall go over it once more. There is no subsidy paid on imported bituminous coal. A small subsidy, in the neighbourhood of twenty-five cents a ton, is paid on anthracite coal.

When item 3 was
reached this afternoon I was in the railway and shipping committee. I wish to thank the minister and the committee for permitting me to discuss the question of Wartime Housing at this time. Each year since Wartime Housing was organized I have discussed the activities of this important crown company. I have made my critical remarks on the score that the cost per unit was excessive, that temporary houses were being built in centres where an acute shortage of permanent houses existed, and that slum areas were being created. However, my protestations were not successful in changing the government's policy. The building activities of Wartime Housing are coming to an end, and therefore I do not think any good purpose will be served by a further reiteration of the points I have made in previous years.
I should like to say, however, that I believe the people of Canada appreciate the fact that the federal government recognized that a serious shortage of housing in the early stages of the war was having an injurious effect on our war production. The people also appreciate the fact that living quarters provided by Wartime Housing were more satisfactory than other quarters available at comparable rents in the centres where Wartime Housing have carried on their activities. It is unfortunate that, after having spent over 870,000,000 and after having built over seventeen thousand units, the Department of Munitions and Supply is not making some plan to extend the activities of this corporation into the post-war period or making some plans to have some government agency prepared to go into the field of providing housing accommodation for people in the lower income brackets, people who cannot hope to find suitable living quarters provided by the private builder. In this country as

War Appropriation-Supplies

in every other country at least one-third of the families are not receiving in peace time and in war time an income sufficiently large to enable them to pay an economic rent. As a consequence, society must provide substantial sums of money every year to maintain slum areas. We pay for these areas in one way or another. At the present time in Canada we are paying to maintain our slum areas through excessive fire protection costs, excessive juvenile delinquency costs, excessive police protection costs, the excessive cost of hospital and medical services to care for people living in slums.
Just before Christmas I had the good fortune to visit a number of centres in the United States where the public authorities have embarked upon slum clearing projects. I understand that the general manager and president of Wartime Housing also visited some of these centres, and after I have finished I should like to hear something from the minister in regard to any reports he may have received from these gentlemen. The committee might be interested to hear something of the development in the city of Boston, for example. I understand that the minister was a student at M.I.T. a number of years ago, and possibly he will recall the very large slum area out in the Charlestown district. If you go to this area and drive down Bunker Hill you will find on one side of the street the century old slums that have been a disgrace to that country for so long, and on the other side a twenty-five acre plot where the slum dwellings have been levelled to the ground and modern fireproof apartment buildings erected, so designed that every family has sunlight at some time during the day. They have running water, frigidaire, heat and light, all supplied by the Boston housing authority, which is supported partly by federal funds and partly by funds of the city of Boston. The housing authority was required to build according to certain regulations, which stipulated that the cost of a housing unit should not exceed a specified amount. Consequently the units are more crowded than people accustomed to the wide open spaces of Canada might wish, but the remarkable thing is that living quarters have been provided at such reasonable rentals. A family enjoying an income of $750 a year can rent a modern four-room apartment foT $15 a month, with light, heat and other services supplied. A larger family occupying a five-room house would pay $16 a month. If you had a larger income you would pay $24. The largest apartments, which have six rooms, rent for from $17 to $25 per month, and in all cases the rental includes light, heat and all other services. In addition to these very comfortable quarters, people living in the project

have access to playgrounds so that children may be kept away from heavy traffic. In the summer time the children may use wading pools, and fountains play while they bask in the sunlight. In the fall of the year the boys play rugby on the project grounds. At three o'clock I found some of the children, whose parents were working in war industries, in a bright room under the supervision of a trained nurse. Three of the little tots were fast asleep on cots provided by the authority. At four o'clock I saw the children hurrying from school to the library, which is located in the basement of one of the buildings; in another room teen-age girls were being taught sewing, while in the community theatre the boys were rehearsing a minstrel ' show. It is true that the federal government provides a subsidy to bridge the difference between the rents paid by the people in the community and the cost of amortizing the entire project over a sixty-year period, at very low interest rates, but my information is that if the cost of maintaining those slum areas were taken into consideration the federal subsidy would be of very small proportions.
Near Washington there is another project that is of great interest. I refer to the Green-belt community, twelve miles from the centre of Washington. Again federal funds were used to make it possible for people in the low income brackets to have up-to-date, convenient quarters at rents averaging not more than twenty per cent of their monthly income. Several thousand acres of farm land were purchased at a low cost and a modem community has been planned, with something over one thousand units to begin with; but recently the size of the project has been doubled. The housing units are situated around the rim of a horseshoe, in the form of a garden city, with underpasses under busy thoroughfares, which make it possible for the children to travel from home to school in safety. Shopping areas have been planned as part of the project, and the people living in the community have been allowed to operate their own cooperative stores in buildings erected with federal funds. It is true that the cost per unit in the Greenbelt area has been higher than in most other centres in the United States, but experimental work has been carried on there which will be of real value in the post-war period.
I appreciate that with Canada at war, the Minister of Munitions and Supply could not have been expected to build houses of the style of those in the Greenbelt area, but greater precaution might have been taken to see that the rows upon rows of houses erected in Canada should not have been built in areas

War Appropriation-Supplies
where there is a serious shortage of permanent houses, and where the tendency will be for these units to develop into slum areas. I do not see how this parliament can separate the work which has been done by Wartime Housing from the work which must be done very soon by some department of government to provide homes for those who are fighting for our freedom. It was originally planned that the houses built by Wartime Housing would be demolished within six months after the conclusion of the war. I should like to remind the committee that seventy thousand people are occupying these houses at the present time and that with very few exceptions, which would be in isolated places where war industries have been located, there is a serious shortage of houses in every centre. It just would not be practical to ask these seventy thousand people to move to the parks or on to the streets while their houses were being demolished in order that the terms of the contract might be fulfilled. It seems to me that now, when we are having layoffs in many industries, many of those who otherwise may be in the ranks of the unemployed should be able to find work in providing suitable housing in strategic centres of this country, as part of a national, provincial or federal plan.'
Unfortunately governments in Canada have not had very much imagination in dealing with housing needs. In my province we had some experience in rural housing when hon. gentlemen to my right were in office a number of years ago. Several hundred families were reestablished in the northern part of Saskatchewan during the depression years, when a great many builders were out of work and Canada's construction programme was practically at a standstill. The most ambitious rural housing programme that the federal and provincial authorities could provide in those days called for an expenditure of $50 per unit. Of course the logs were available, free for the cutting; but all the hardware, windows, shingles and flooring had to be purchased with the $50. It does not require much imagination to visualize the type of quarters built for hundreds of families in Saskatchewan under the plan worked out jointly by the Bennett government in Ottawa and the Anderson government in Regina.
When I was home at Christmas I stayed in one of those $50 homes, located twenty-seven miles from the nearest railway station and the nearest doctor. The family living there had enjoyed prosperity in Saskatchewan some years ago. They had gone north in the early thirties when the drought and the depression 100-122J
made prospects in the south look very dull. While they are having more prosperous days now than they had when they first came in, they are still living in the $50 house. They do not know whether to go back to the prairies or whether to stay, in the hope that conditions may improve.
In Saskatchewan we had a change in government in 1934, and there was a change at Ottawa in 1935. More generous housing programmes were then introduced. The ceiling for rural housing was increased from $50 to $75. This increase did make possible a considerable improvement in living quarters. It meant that one could put shingles on the roof, instead of slabs from the nearest sawmill. But I hope that people in Canada will not be compelled to live in a country where $50 or even $75 houses are the order of the day.
I find that two valuable reports have recently been released in the United States, dealing with their immediate housing needs. One, by the C.I.O., is entitled "A Housing Programme for an Economy of Abundance." It points out that the primary responsibility for filling shelter needs of the people of the United States is a public one which must be met by government action. They call for 500,000 units of so-called public housing a year, and more if private housing fails to do its job. That is the whole question -whether private builders can make good their boast and be able to make good the housing needs of the country. If they cannot, public housing and cooperative housing will have to take that responsibility.
Further on in the report they say:
In respect to shelter, such production levels call for a completely new orientation. The fundamental question will no longer be: What kind of housing can we afford? The issue before us will be: What kind of housing, within reason, do we desire? . . .
The conditions of life which have dictated this attitude of submission to private interest and accidental circumstance no longer exist. It will shortly be within our power to determine for ourselves the nature of all the surroundings amid which we live our lives.
Then, Harry C. Bates, chairman of the housing committee of the American Federation of Labor presented before the house committee on public buildings and grounds in Washington on February 10, 1944, a most interesting brief. In it he says:
Housing has long remained the most neglected part in the improvement of the American standard of living through either private or public action. Before the war we were too far behind in the volume of housing construction to even hope to catch up with the need in the near future. The war has set us back even farther.
