Then he points out it was not until trade union leaders forced the issue that a national survey was carried out in 1940, to find out really what the housing situation was in the United States. They found that:
A dwelling either in need of major repairs or without a private toilet or private bath, was classed as substandard. If the American standard of living means anything, this test is certainly sound. The census showed that in 1940 in our town and cities alone there were over 6 million homes classed as substandard by this test. In addition, there were over 5 million non-farm homes in rural communities in this substandard condition. To top this we also had nearly 7 million farm dwellings which failed to measure up to this simple minimum standard. In the case of farm homes, even if we disregard the absence of sanitary facilities, 34 per cent or over 2J million farm houses, were in unsafe and unlivable substandard condition.
We have not gone as far as they have in the United States. We have not compiled any accurate statistics showing the number of housing units built in Canada in the thirties. While some progress was made'in connection with the 1941 census, there still is not available in Canada any satisfactory picture of the housing needs of the country.
However, I must congratulate the government upon making a start. I have not had a chance to look at the very large volume tabled to-day by the Prime Minister, but the table of contents suggests that it is at least a start. I find in the contents a reference to housing legislation in Canada, housing legislation in Great Britain and in the United States, urban housing, post-war housing needs, town planning, home ownership and related programmes, low rental housing, farm housing, reduction in housing costs, and so on. I hope that this report may be printed and made available to hon. members and those who are interested, as are other reports which have been tabled by the Prime Minister.
It is only a report.

I am glad the hon. member mentions it is just a report. It is on paper, and I think at this stage we should be much farther along than we apparently are, if any action is to be expected in time to meet serious trouble in the post-war period.
Before concluding, I should like to congratulate, as other hon. members have done, the Minister of Munitions and Supply upon the imaginative job he has done since taking over his portfolio. Only members of his department and members of parliament who have had an opportunity to travel from coast to coast and to visit some of the war industries have any adequate appreciation of what has been done in his department. But I would

suggest that if the minister would like to make a permanent name for himself in the annals of Canadian history, he might do so by showing the same imagination in facing up to a housing programme for the years which are to come. He might be able to keep the present government in office, and he would find thousands of people across this country who, for the first time in a lifetime, would be able to say, "Well, at last we are able to have a decent house, thanks to C. D. Howe."
But this is not going to happen by accident. Unless the minister is going to make plans and spend funds in the same reckless fashion as has obtained in connection with the huge expenditures which have been made for war purposes, his munitions achievements will have been forgotten in a very few years. It is only natural that many people working in these industries see the local problems, and find it difficult to see the larger picture of Canada's production.	They know something of the
bottlenecks. They know something of the problems which develop when materials have not moved along in time, and when it seemed as though they were being paid for very little work. But I thing, if we look at their picture, we shall understand that and appreciate the difficulties experienced. Those who are working in these large industries will not remember very long the Minister of Munitions and Supply, who has provided leadership in this particular field. But if he could carry out the programme suggested by the Minister of Labour, that of having 100,000 houses built each year for the next ten years, he would have a million families in Canada in a ten-year period, or 100,000 a year who would be living in better quarters than ever before. I do not think there is a chance in the world to have such a programme carried out by private industry or by the machinery set up under national housing. I need only remind the committee that in the past under its activities our best performance was about 6,000 houses a year and a total of 25,000 houses for some eight years. Wartime Housing has built only 17,000 houses in two and a half years, or at the rate of less than 10,000 houses a year. How small this total is when compared with the figure of
100.000	houses used by the Minister of Labour.
I should like now to make some recommendations to the minister. A conference should be called immediately at which provincial, municipal and federal authorities could discuss housing problems exclusively. I think one of the mistakes that Wartime Housing made was to fail to recognize that under the British North America Act certain powers belong to the federal government, certain powers belong to the provincial government

War Appropriation-Supplies
and certain powers belong to the municipal government. No federal authority should ride roughshod over either the provincial or the municipal authority without due consultation.
My second recommendation is that plans be made for a complete revamping of the National Housing Act and reorganization of the national housing administration. , When the government found it necessary to build houses to meet war-time needs, for some reason or another the staff at national housing administration headquarters were not satisfactory. That was a question of government policy. If the national housing administration staff were not sufficiently efficient in 1941, some policy should be laid down by the government for a reorganization which would make available a satisfactory administration.
A research staff should be set up to go into the different aspects of housing and find out whether home ownership is the only method that should be adopted. They should find out whether there is not a place for low rent houses and they should do some work on town planning. Consideration should be given to the improvement of rural housing, for of all our houses in Canada those which cry out most loudly for improvement are our farm homes. Plans should be made for the extension of the home improvement plan and research should be carried on in building designs. A recent number of Engineering and Contract Record contains an article in connection with increasing the efficiency of the construction industry. Men in the construction industry are seriously considering new techniques that must be used if Canada is to keep pace with modern trends and modern requirements. They suggest that research should be carried on for the manufacturer with a view to (a) Eliminating duplication in stock sizes; (b) A solution for the problem of standardization which various industries manufacturing building supplies are trying to solve individually; (c) A stimulated demand for stock sizes in preference to special sizes, as a result of their more convenient and economical field erection; (d) Lower costs of manufacturing against stock as compared with the custom manufacture of special sizes and details; (e) Improved precision and uniformity of quality that result from improved manufacturing processes; (f) A market for standardized building materials where the cost of special detailing or field cutting would be prohibitive; (g) Standard assembly details which would help the manufacturer to control the installation of his products and thus avoid complaints that arise from faulty workmanship. Research is suggested also for the architect and the builder and contractor as well as for the consumer.
If the cost of housing can be reduced, more houses will be built and more contented Canadians will be living in them. I notice the national housing administration and the code and specifications section of the national research council have put out an interesting book on the national building code. However, it seems rather difficult to secure a copy of this book. This is one of the few instances where I have asked for a copy of a publication and been requested to state whether it is for myself. That is a most unusual question to be asked by any government authority issuing a publication. Publications like this should be supplied to members of parliament as a matter of course.
Could the minister make some statement as to what the plans are at this stage with regard to disposing of the 17,000 houses built by Wartime Housing? Could he give a report to the committee in connection with the findings of the president and general manager of public housing in the United States? Has any consideration been given to retaining the staff of Wartime Housing with a view to having them engage in the type of research I have outlined?

It has been the duty of this deparment to find housing for employees in war industries, in order to make sure that war industries can operate efficiently. The government as a whole is greatly absorbed in the matter of a post-war housing. Other departments are conducting studies of the type referred to by my hon. friend. I do not know that the complete post-war programme of the government can be announced, but I think I am safe in saying that the housing of Canadian citizens will have an important part in that programme.
My hon. friend asked _what our plans are for the disposing of war-time houses after the war. Our agreement with practically every municipality in which wartime houses have been built provides that at the end of the war, the houses will be dismantled and moved away. I am not sure just what will be done when that day comes. These are quite comfortable houses, and I imagine that the eventual disposal will be to put good basements under them, install heating plants and regard them as permanent houses. However, that will be up to each individual municipality. The government will be prepared to carry out its agreement if the municipality so

desires. With that uncertainty, it would be quite improper for me to discuss any disposition of the houses, other than to carry out the agreements which stipulate that the houses will be removed1 at the end of the war.

I understand from the minister that the programme of Wartime Housing is almost completed, and I should like to know if he is retaining the staff and, if so, what type of work he has in mind for them to do from now on?

The staff of Wartime Housing has been reduced, to some extent. This has not been done deliberately; the reduction has taken place in this staff as in all staffs which are not being expanded. My hon. friend will understand that there is a considerable administration work involved in operating our housing projects. Studies have been made in the past, along the lines suggested by my hon. friend, and these will be made available to whatever department assumes responsibility for the post-war programme. I have no doubt that a number of the staff of Wartime Housing will be needed by the department which takes this programme in hand. In my opinion the staff of Wartime Housing has been most efficient, and has used excellent judgment in its operations. Personally I would' be sorry if the talents of that organization are not used to the fullest extent.

The minister has referred to the possible cessation of the activities of Wartime Housing. Will this apply to Malton, for instance, where staff houses are to be erected in connection with the influx of further employees in the Victory aircraft plant?

My hon. friend will have
noticed that we put in an additional one million dollar appropriation. When I said that the programme had ended, I did not mean a sharp cut-off. We have a small provision for new facilities that may be required, and Malton is a place where new facilities may be required. ,We have a programme there which will be going on for some time. The need for housing reaches somewhat beyond the local situation. If the employees are housed in Toronto, and are moved to Malton by rail, we shall not require additional facilities at Malton; but if we move in new em

ployees from a distance, requiring additional housing there, housing will be built.

I realize that the minister
is not responsible for the administration of the national housing act, and that his department is not responsible for the administration of the home improvement loan plan. But is

it not a fact that restrictions on building materials come under the Department of Munitions and Supply?
Yes.

I believe that a little less
than a year ago the department placed restrictions on the building of homes, making it practically impossible at that time to get the materials required for home building. More recently some change has been made in those restrictions, presumably as supplies became available. Could the minister tell the committee this evening just what the present position is with regard to the availability of supplies and equipment for building homes in Canada? Then we shall have a better idea of what can be done now in the way of starting to rehouse the Canadian people. I urge upon-the minister that he review these restrictions again to see whether it would not be possible to relax or wipe out altogether some of these restrictions. If that were done, private contractors would greatly increase the number of homes built, and many of our people would be given some place to live. The minister realizes, I suppose, just as well as the rest of the hon. members do, that the present housing situation is very difficult. People are living in garrets, garages and basements, and whole families are living in one room. This must have an effect on the war effort because it lowers the morale of our people, and I am sure it is seriously injuring the health of the Canadian people as a whole. In addition, it would be very difficult under present conditions to reestablish the men who come back from the war. . I would be the last one to urge any action that would interfere with the war effort, but surely the time has now come when we should start on a deliberate campaign to rehouse the Canadian people. It would be well worth while. In some centres-I know it is the case in Vancouver, here in Ottawa and certainly in Halifax-the positon is almost impossible. Some consideration might be given to declaring certain areas emergency areas and allowing special housing provisions to be made applicable there. The policy of the department has been to encourage the building of small homes to the full extent that the materials situation would permit. Even in the days of greatest scarcity, the department has recognized emergent situations in particular localities and has diverted available supplies of materials to those areas in preference to less urgent areas. The shortages to-day are

more particularly bathroom fittings, and certain other essential components of a modern home. That is, permanent small
homes?

Yes. We do not wish to
encourage the undertaking of home building that cannot be carried out for lack of materials. That is not helpful to anyone. I can assure my hon. friend that we shall take steps to encourage home building just as soon as we can increase the supply of materials.

Would it be possible to
arrange for some factories in Canada to step up the production of bathroom fittings and other materials in short supply, just as was done with certain urgently required war materials?

Is there any intention of extending the provisions of the National Housing Act so that ninety per cent instead of the present eighty per cent can be borrowed from the government for the building of a home? Is there any prospect of having the interest rate on the loans reduced?

I understand that a new
national housing act will be brought down this session, and I would prefer my hon. friend to obtain the information when the bill is brought down.

Mr. Chairman, I would draw the attention of the government and of parliament to a grievance of a serious nature.
I refer to the disastrous situation falling upon the producers of maple syrup and maple sugar caused by the new regulations of the wartime prices and trade board.
The rationing of these products and the necessity for the producer to request coupons from consumers means that the producer either cannot develop his sugar bush or can sell only a very small portion of his products.
On March 13 last, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in asnwering questions I put on the orders of the day, stated that Canada exported during 1943 only 3,959,647 pounds of maple sugar and 181,596 gallons of maple syrup. Why, then, ration these products in Canada? There is no reason for doing so. Therefore I request the government to redress immediately this unfortunate state of affairs caused by the rationing of maple products both for -the producers and for the consumers.
(Translation): There is another matter with which I desire to deal briefly. It is the necessity of sending back to the farm all farmers at present in the army. If the army and the civilian population are to obtain necessary supplies, it is imperative to take such a step.
Agriculture is deprived of more than 600,000 workers, male and female. These persons were absorbed by the army and by war industries. However, the government continues to call up farmers' sons for training. Even when they have been granted deferments, they must undergo another medical examination which is given the ridiculous name of "revision." When will the authorities realize that more than ever agriculture needs all available help? Why did they not leave the medical examinations of called-up men to the family physician, as was formerly the case? No matter how well qualified he may be, a medical officer can never replace the family physician who is well acquainted with the personal history of the men who are called up. Thus, the government causes a heavy loss of time to agriculture and to over-burdened farmers. Must I once more point out to the government that agriculture is in urgent need of help and that it would be preferable to return to civilian life all the farmers now in the army? This would be one of the best ways to avoid the numberless pitfalls of the post-war period. In the course of the transition period, for which we should prepare immediately, agriculture must play a major part in the world's economic reestablishment. Losing sight of these facts would constitute a fatal mistake. Let us now return to the land those farmers who have been forced to forsake it on account of the war.

Mr. Chairman, before closing my remarks, I shall quote an extract from Hansard of March 30, 1939. In it the Right Hon. Prime Minister (M r. Mackenzie King) opposes Canadian participation in the war. Let us not forget, that he made this speech only five months before his government assumed a share in the world conflict and before they bought two destroyers from Great Britain. Here are the words of the head of the present government, on this occasion, as reported on page 2426 of Hansard for 1939:
One strategic fact is clear: the days of great expeditionary forces of infantry crossing the ocean are not likely to recur. Two years ago, I expressed in this house the view that it was extremely doubtful if any of the British dominions would ever send another expeditionary force to Europe.
He had previously said, as may be seen on page 2419:
We have tremendous tasks to do at home, in housing the people, in caring for the aged and helpless, in relieving drought and unemployment, in building roads, in meeting our heavy burden of debt. . . .
At that time it stood at one and a half billion dollars.
... in making provision for Canada's defence, and in bringing our standards of living and civilization to the levels our knowledge now makes possible.
_ Mr. Chairman, was there, at that time, a single hon. member who did not realize that the increased military estimates were being voted not only to ensure the defence of Canada but also with a view to participating in foreign wars I repeated that statement time and again, at that period. The right hon. Prime Minister added:
There is no great margin of realizable wealth for this purpose; we must, to a greater or less extent, choose between keeping our own house in order and trying to save Europe and Asia.
How can one reconcile such a solemn statement uttered by the Prime Minister with the actions by which he followed it a few weeks later? For my part, I have kept faith with the word I had pledged. I have long since withdrawn from that atmosphere strewn with falsehood.
Let him who laughs interrupt me and ask me a single question on the position I have taken. Does the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Gingues) wish to do so? Let him go ahead!
All in good time.

Do those who, on September 9, 1939, did not lift a finger in support of my amendment against participation in war, feel satisfied now with their doings?

At this stage of my remarks I must recognize the Canadian spirit, the loyalty and the honesty of the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. LaCroix), who alone supported me. Is any satisfaction felt by our colleagues who voted for the mobilization act on June 19, 1940, overwhelming my amendment by a vote of 202 against 2? On that occasion the hon. member for Quebec-Mont-morency was again alone in supporting me. Do our colleagues derive any satisfaction from what they have done? '
I am blaming neither the government supporters in this house nor the opposition, but I do blame the hypocritical members who denied us their support and who divided us on that question. I have more compliments to offer to the government supporters than to the opposition. I remind those members that they protected, in their own way, our young men and our farmers, by mobilizing and conscripting them. They are now protesting against a dreadful situation which they have themselves brought about, of their own free will and wittingly. The time will soon come, Mr. Chairman, when we shall let the people know about the devious and knavish stand of the false prophets of the day. The people do not know them yet. We will put them in the limelight. My first duty is to denounce the would-be patriots who have left nothing undone in order to foment disunion among true Canadians, especially in the province of Quebec-as was pointed out by the right hon. the prime minister - not only some time ago but during the last few sessions. Divide and govern, such was their only goal. They care not a whit about disinterestedness, and sincerity is .with them a lacking virtue. Their patriotism is limited to fine speeches broadcast over the air lanes. Open at random the debates of the house and you will be amazed at the unmatched hypocrisy of these elected representatives who are responsible for the distressing situation which prevails in agriculture and all over civilian industry in Canada. To all these sham patriots, I prefer a man sincere, honest and true who faces his opponent squarely and strives against policies he cannot countenance.

As I said last year, tlie housing situation in Toronto is still bad. If any more people come to the city we shall have to have war-time housing. Toronto has never had any war-time housing. The only thing we have had is some money to convert a few apartments. I am glad to

This evening I
intend to refer to the address of the minister on March 17 in connection with the subject of post-war aviation. The minister's speech unfolded a pattern and formula for international control, coupled with a draft international convention, timely because the questions raised are in a state of flux at this time and also because nations all over the world are formulating conventions and making plans for the post-war solution of this great problem.
In its domestic as in its international aspects the enunciation of policy was made by the minister without benefit of discussion in parliament. I make that statement without any wish to enter into a political discussion, for I believe that a debate on this important matter should be free of any partisan considerations, and that discussion should be constructively designed to advance the cause of post-war aviation. The minister properly referred to the history of civil aviation and sketched something of the progress of the past few years in connection with the development of

War Appropriation-Transport

airways, for without a knowledge of the past and of the incidents that have occurred since the last war this subject becomes even more difficult of comprehension.
As I see it, the problem divides itself into three classes or aspects, namely the international and, within the international, our relationship to the United States of America; second, the interempire or commonwealth relationship, and, finally, the domestic relationship. To-day we find ourselves, as does the world, on the threshold of a great evolutionary change in world commerce. A third dimension has been established in world travel; hours, not miles, are now the measure of distance. The result is that isolationism and the sense of security that was based on oceanic barriers are to-day as dead as belief in the invulnerability of the Chinese wall. This is a tremendous problem. As far as I am concerned I have not had the advantage of the help of technicians in carrying on research, but I found the discussion by the minister most interesting and most complete, and I must pay my compliments to those who assisted him in the preparation of the draft convention. Air transport has no antiquity; only the future can tell the degree and extent of its impact upon civilization. To base a policy now on prophecy is out of the question. We must face the problems as we see them to-day, as they are now; and in evolving a policy provision must be made for changes and developments as they may become necessary.
One general criticism I offer as to the policy announced by the minister is that it is too inflexible, rigid and uncompromising to meet the needs of a problem as comprehensive and changing as the air problem. There are some matters upon which there is general agreement as, for instance, Canada's strategic position in the routing of international traffic west to the orient, east to the continent of Europe and north to Europe and Asia. While this factor may be too greatly emphasized, on the other hand I take it that hon. members on all sides of this house are now in agreement that Canada must not allow herself to become in the modern world what Asia Minor was in past ages, an area to be crossed over by other nations or, in the present era, an area to be flown over. I believe we all agree that an international set-up controlling aviation is indicated as the only solution of this problem in its broad aspects. Every country has its own particular problems. Every country has its political, military and economic interests in air transport, for 'all recognize to-day that while planes carry passengers they also carry bombs. After the last war, in spite of the many conferences that took place, nations

refused to accept the principles of freedom of transit and international control, with the result that air development was obstructed internationally. Competition in Europe was between France, the Netherlands and Germany; in the east it was between Britain, France and the Netherlands, while in South America Germany achieved a wide measure of control. Prior to this war the attitude of most nations was that air lines were arteries of national policy and empire, and all nations, in their own Interests and in the interests of their defence, claimed ownership of the air above their territories. Commercial planes of all nations were denied the right to pass over or land in foreign countries, even for rest, refuge or refueling, except by agreement. The right to take on or discharge passengers or traffic was a matter of national policy. The attitude of the nations in this way was that national exclusion rather than international cooperation prevailed, and that deterred development of the airways between 1919 and 1939. All plane companies in Europe were controlled by the state, directly or indirectly, and air transport was a phase of national development. In the United States private ownership was encouraged to develop airways, and at the outbreak of the war no country in the world had a civil system of air transport in excess of that developed in the United States.
I am not going into details of the various routes which were established by nations in Europe and beyond. Suffice it to say this, that restrictions were universal, because nations feared the destructiveness of air power rather than the benefits to mankind in its extension. For example, the United States refused rights to foreign airways to fly over Hawaii. In a route of one thousand miles from Lisbon to Warsaw, there were four changes of planes. United States planes had to discharge their passengers in Ireland en joute to Britain, and take other planes to complete their journey to their destination. The fear of bombs, the distrust between nations, and nationalistic policies designed to deny international control, built up an international philosophy of non-cooperation and restriction. ,
Possible disagreements between nations and the necessity for air transport being made available everywhere in the world make international control desirable and necessary; for history teaches that if aviation is to be nationally controlled on a narrow basis, the seeds of a future war to secure freedom of transit or freedom of the air will have been planted.

Aviation, properly controlled, can be made mankind's handmaiden for peace; uncontrolled, it will remain a potential destroyer of mankind.
I think no better summary of the matter can be found than in a recent book, "The Air Future", in which the author, Burnet Hershey, said this:
The important thing to remember about aviation is its universal character. It can be destructively annihilating or almost superhumanly beneficent; but it can never be subjected to localized restriction. To aviation political boundaries are obsolete absurdities. Above the clouds the earth itself is out of sight, and at 400 miles an hour the crossing of an imaginary line drawn arbitrarily across an invisible planet far beneath, is of less consequence to pilot and passenger than the blowing of the wind and the direction of the wind.
The difference between freedom of the air and freedom of transit is that between licence and liberty. The war's outcome is even now being determined by the superiority of air power, and I believe that air transport after the war may well determine the future of mankind. I agree with the minister's viewpoint that international freedom, rather than selfish national aspirations, must be the foundation stone upon which a new world order will be built. In enunciating an international air policy at this time Canada has assured the world that, as far as she is concerned, located on the airways of the world, occupying a position unequalled in those airways, she intends not to allow herself to become a national instrument for international rivalry, but means to devote herself to the principles of peace, through international action. To this end there will have to be international recognition by all nations, and there is the inescapable fact that the experience in the twentieth century is that no nation can live unto itself alone while desirous of trading by air with other nations.
That brings me to a principle which is rather difficult to understand, namely the doctrine of freedom of transit or freedom of innooent passage, sometimes mistakenly called freedom of the air. Britain calls it the open sky, as distinguished from the sovereignty of air policy, the closed sky policy. Freedom of the air denies international control, when freedom of the air is used in its wider sense. It means that the atmosphere is open to the planes of all nations without control. What that would mean is again set out in the same book to which I referred a moment ago, in these words:
In essence freedom of the air means exactly the same thing as freedom of the road, the free right of the driver of any motor vehicle to use any road anywhere on earth without buying
any licence, taking any operator's examination, or otherwise submitting to any regulation in the interest of public safety. Such a state of anarchy applied to surface transportation is ' obviously absurd. It is even more ridiculous when carried to the skies.
Much discussion has taken place on this principle, and it seems now generally agreed that freedom of the right of transit should be recognized by all nations, great and small, but that the right of foreign nations to take on cargoes and passengers must remain a matter of agreement between nations affected. Those who desire freedom of the air at once must remember that it took more than 350 years to establish the somewhat correlative doctrine of freedom of the seas. The adoption of freedom of the air to-day, in its widest sense, would in my opinion destroy Canada's chance of participation on a world basis, in international airways. Canada would be put in competition with subsidized airways of countries operating national routes. I should like to ask the minister what provision is made in the convention, and what his ideas are in connection with the matter of preventing or at least controlling subsidization by nations of the air routes which are set up. Freedom of the air is impossible, if national safety is to be considered. On the other hand, the closed sky policy is not open to Canada to adopt, because of the danger to international peace that such a policy would result in. The intermediate principle of freedom of transit would appear to be the solution.
The minister, in speaking the other day,
used these words at page 1579 of Hansard:
Each nation should at least possess the right to carry passengers and cargo from its own territory to other countries, and to bring back from those other countries passengers and cargo which are intended for its own territory.
With that view I disagree for, in my opinion, it is altogether too wide in its scope. The adoption of this principle would destroy the possibility of the Canadian air industry drawing a fair share of cross-frontier traffic. Take our position during the past few years, when we have had an equality with the United States of America on trans-frontier routes. Yet to-day we operate but one route, compared with eight operated by the United States of America into Canada. Experience in the operation of the airways during recent years between these two countries denies the application of the principle enunciated by the minister respecting our relations with the United States of America.
I believe that the principle of an international air transport authority rather than an international air transport system represents the viewpoint of the people of this nation, as

I protest against the principle of setting up boards with judicial functions, and at the same time denying them independence and power to carry out the recommendations that they make. As far as the general principle in Canada's domestic airways is concerned, the minister has adopted the principle that TCA shall have exclusive authority in so far as the Trans-Canada routes are concerned. The minister says that there is an opportunity to private enterprise in the feeder routes and accordingly the government recognizes the necessity of competition. Is the government going to subsidize these young men who come back from overseas? How are these young men to finance, themselves in the setting up of these air routes? What provision is to be made for inter-city traffic? Is that to be under the government? The other day I read an article which indicated that during the next few months it is expected that there will be established in the United States a helicopter set-up, and that there are over some thousand applications for routes on hand to date. Will there be such a development in Canada? If so, will it be under government control?
The minister stated at page 1574 of Hansard of March 17, 1944:
A vigorous aeroplane construction industry is an essential complement to Canada's post-war aviation plans.
Where will the demand be' for these planes? How many of the factories are to be maintained? How many of the men will be employed? The minister says that the railways companies must dissociate themselves from air expansion. He will be able to explain the reason for that, no doubt, for the explanation that he has given so far does not fit very well into the explanation that he gave in 1937 when he said that the airways should be under the railway corporations.
What is the attitude in Britain? They are changing their attitude. They are giving the railway companies an opportunity to expand air services within the country and even on to the continent. The United States has declared for private ownership as far as foreign airways are concerned, although it is believed that so far as transoceanic airways are concerned they will be pooled .as between the various companies. I ask this question: Where are the young men coming back from overseas to secure the opportunity that is promised them by the minister in the air development of the future unless there is continued in this country private enterprise alongside of state development? In my opinion, imagination, resourcefulness and initiative can come only

War Appropriation-Transport
through a degree of competition, wherein the best benefits are secured from both state and private enterprise. There are fields for both. There is need of both, but there should be rigid control to prevent abuse, to assure com* petition in the interests of efficiency and to control monopoly. The rights of companies to develop new routes with reasonable service and at reasonable prices should be encouraged; and assurance should be given that the companies that develop shall be subject not to penalization when they have success, but to a continuation in the work that they have undertaken so long as they furnish good, efficient service at reasonable rates.
There is a definite change in the attitude of the minister in regard to railways. In 1937, the minister announced his views as reported in Hansard at page 2216. At that time he set out the reasons why the railway companies should operate. Why has he changed his views? These are matters on which we should like to have information. What has happened that has resulted in the necessity for the divestment of railway companies of their airway interests? Without the minister's answer to that question we cannot discuss the matter at any great length. Suffice it to say that, as far as this party is concerned, we believe that Canada should maintain control over the further i developing of her vital position in national and international air transport. We believe that all internal air domestic aviation should remain under the board of transport commissioners or a board with similar powers, and not under the control of the executive. We believe that the existing TCA lines should be maintained and reasonably expanded; that privately owned commercial aviation should be allowed to expand and to open up new routes.
I again wish to thank the committee for having permitted me to speak beyond the forty-minute period. The science of aeronautics has developed in the laboratory of war. It becomes a matter of world importance that it shall be utilized and extended into the world of peace. Canada, with courage and skill and her strategic world position, has earned the opportunity to achieve a great destiny in postwar air development. But I warn this committee that we must be careful in the decision at which we arrive. Hon. members should discuss this problem freely and untrammelled, because we must make sure that Canada becomes more than a cross-roads, for Canada must be a factor in world and empire air development. What I have said is far from the final word that can be said on the subject, as I am sure the minister would admit that what he said was far from the final word.
It is too early yet for anyone to speak with finality on the course of the airways after the war; but frank, free and unprejudiced discussion now may well bring about the creation of a path that will lead Canada to the goal of world peace, empire cooperation and the assurance to the Canadian people of domestic happiness and prosperity.

I am going to take a minute or two, since the hon. member for Lake Centre referred to the statements made in this house by my colleague the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and myself on March 20. The hon. gentleman pointed out, as is done so frequently in this chamber, that we have very niuch in common with the British labour party and the labour parties of the commonwealths of New Zealand and Australia; and he went on to say that the British labour party had taken the position that international ownership as well as international control of the main air routes of the world might be undertaken. Just to keep the record straight, I should like to quote what I said in the course of my remarks, at page 1656 of Hansard:
I think in the field of civil aviation we must have international understanding, international operation and international control. I should like to see the world go beyond where I think it can go to-day. I should like to see an international system owned internationally; but I realize that under present world conditions not only is that improbable but it is quite out of the question. Hence I believe we must have an intergovernmental regulatory body, one which will license and regulate and enter into arrangements with the nations, so that we may achieve the results we desire, namely efficient transportation, rapid transportation, comfortable transportation, safe transportation-and peace at the end of it all.
When that statement was made I was thinking that we do not know where Russia stands, as the hon. member for Lake Centre has said. We read of a considerable discussion of international airways in the United States of America, and it seems-unfortunately, I think -that the best we can hope for from the United States is international control, intergovernmental agreement. While I should like to see a wider scheme, we have to be realistic about the matter and get the best we can. I am glad the government has gone as far as it has in that respect; I wish that it might go farther. I realize there are others who wish to place the views of their particular parties or groups before this committee, so that while I should like to comment farther on what the hon. .member for Lake Centre has said, I do not believe that at this time I should take more of the time of the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I have followed with the greatest interest the question of civil aviation ever since the last war, during which eighteen thousand cadets and mechanics of the Royal 'Air Force were trained in the city of Toronto. After the war many prominent people, including the late Colonel Barker, V.C., Air Marshal Bishop, Sir Frederick Handley Page, Air Marshal Collishaw and others came back to Toronto-and as mayor I discussed the matter with them for months-that Canada, which had done so splendidly in the last war, should continue with a programme of civil aviation during the time of peace. As an example, I refer to the progress that had been made three hundred years before on the high seas, when Britain, of her own volition, went out and created an oceanic empire through sea power, when she had only one rival, Portugal, and later on the Dutch. Britain gained command of the sea and built up her magnificent empire.
I am very much disappointed with the secret policy of the government in this connection. Why did Canada not seek first a conference with the other dominions in order to formulate an empire policy as a unit? What was the need for all this secrecy in regard to a public matter such as this, which is of the utmost importance to the future of the world and the future of our empire? Why were all these star chamber proposals made, when w'e had the minister and his staff in London at a time when there were also in that city representatives of nearly all the countries of the world trying to devise some definite plan for the progress of civil aviation and the progress of the world in general? One objection I have to this internationalization of bases is that Russia, our great ally, will have nothing to do with the idea, because they believe in collectivism. The United States will have nothing to do with internationalization; Washington almost shudders when one mentions it and international aviation. They are going to act separately in civil aviation. It is all very well to come here and appeal for this sort of thing, but after all we are only a nation of ten million people. Why should we go outside the empire and make international treaties with these world powers on one of the most important matters ever to come before the people of this country? It is dangerous to plan to share these bases with any other and give them sovereignty, while allowing user. I referred to this matter on July 15 of last year, when the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce were under consideration. At page 4868 of Hansard I said:
If we had had an international policy which meant the giving up of empire ports like Gibraltar and Suez, the Cape, the far east and

the West Indies, where would we be to-day? The empire would have been destroyed, and that would have meant the fall of civilization.
Already we have given the United States bases for ninety-nine years, reaching from Newfoundland to British Guiana, and no doubt they will want to hold on to them. Let us see what that will mean to this country. The bases which it is proposed to share are the backbone of the British empire on the seven seas. Upon them the security of the British empire has depended for some two hundred years, as it will depend in the future. Just fancy what would have happened to the mother country in the present war without these bases! The commonwealths and colonies would be adrift; the empire would become a perfect absurdity on the map; it would be a body without arteries. Just imagine what would have happened in 1940 if we had been compelled to share Gibraltar, Malta, the Cape, Alexandria and these other bases around the seven seas with the United States and Russia, two neutral powers for two years, and all the other powers that were afraid to provoke Germany. Our position would have been impossible. We should have been under pressure to keep neutral. Internationalization presupposes a perfect world of the future. It is one of those dangerous principles. The policy of the government is one of the most dangerous for the mother country that we have had in the last two hundred years. We are prepared to let trusted allies use our bases, as I said on July 15 last-even in peace. But beyond that concession there are dangers. We have to get back and look at the basic principles behind this policy of internationalization. We have to stop and listen, and go back to the very concept of the British nation, united and strong, to defend itself as a unit, existing as an influence among the powers of the world, and ready to cooperate with others on a self-respecting and honourable basis.
Imperial defence should be strengthened. I spoke in the house on July 15 last, after April 2, when the Prime Minister announced the policy which, in my opinion, has prevented an empire conference since then on this important matter of civil aviation. Civil aviation is to be the transport of the future. The Prime Minister practically threw cold water on the whole thing through the following words, which have been quoted in the British House of Commons. He said on April 2:
The Canadian government strongly favours a policy of international collaboration and cooperation in air transport and is prepared to support in international negotiations whatever international air transport policy can be demonstrated as being best calculated to serve not

War Appropriation-Transport
only the immediate national interests of Canada but also our overriding interest in the establishment of an international order which will prevent the outbreak of another world war.
What was the result of that policy, which was quoted in England, in the British House of Commons? In my opinion, it was quoted by the acting leader of the government as one of the reasons why no empire conference on civil aviation should be called. True it is that some time in October, I believe it is the minister and some of his staff went over and had a conference over there. But there were no practical results from that conference. It was said then that under the statute of Westminster each of the dominions is responsible for its home defence, to three miles outside boundary lines. In addition to that, each dominion retains its status, autonomy and sovereignty, and has to look after its own domestic affairs. So much is that so that even in its air policy the domestic policy of Canada is that, following the statute of Westminster we are to set up a vast monopoly in this country, with hidden subsidies, something which will lead to untold error in connection with this work of civil aviation.
I referred to this speech of the Prime Minister when, speaking in the house on July 15 last, I said that the domestic policy of Canada in the air should be based on a well known policy in navigation laws and lease-lend, and that

We should be ready to cooperate with our allies and allow them to use these air bases, but we should not give away sovereignty over them. The empire has thrown back its enemies from without and in my opinion she will go on to destroy them. Now is the time that we should try to recapture the spirit of empire and our faith and pride in our dominions and in our trade and commerce. The empire is a living thing and should not be allowed to go by default or into liquidation.
That is what you are prepared to do now. You are prepared by this policy to allow this empire to go by default and into liquidation with a war on, instead of being a unit as an empire as to civil aviation. I said further on the same date:
The mother country and the dominions fought this battle alone for two years. Our soldiers carried on with those from India, New Zealand, South Africa, Australia and the empire training plan. We stood shoulder to shoulder in the snows of Labrador and Newfoundland and in the heat of India and the far east.
In the days before the war you could go into any large port and find fifteen or sixteen ships from different parts of the empire carrying on their trade.
I have seen that in Halifax, Victoria and Vancouver.
I believe that this same spirit of empire co-operation will continue in the years that are to come. Canada should be ready to go along
with the dominions and the empire. The time has come when the Minister of Trade and Commerce should tell this committee and the country what our relations are with the other sister dominions who fought along with us for two years to save civilization. One of our great allies stood aside for two years with Germany, but Russia has since made a glorious record. To-day she is practically fighting her battles alone except for some supplies and munitions that are being sent in.
I went on record to the effect that the policy should be to allow these bases to be used by all the world in the future. But sovereignty-no. They should be retained by the mother country and by the British empire. That is why I have objected to such secret policies in the house.
Had the same energy been put into civil aviation in the period between the two wars that has been put into it in the empire air plan since the war started, we never would have had a second war. I have followed this civil aviation question, right from the start of the last war, and I have been very much disappointed in what I have seen.
The minister of Munitions and Supply on the 17th if this month gave a fine history of civil aviation. He placed on record a splendid summary of the progress of civil aviation. He pointed out what had been done by private , enterprise and private initiative. Then he went on to refer to many other matters, pointing out that a reduction had been made in the estimates in 1935, and then went on to a reference to Trans-Canada Air Lines, and how Canadian Pacific Air Lines would not come in.
Did this international agreement he quoted ever come before the other dominions? I am referring to this international agreement given out secretly at Washington, over the heads of parliament, behind our back, when parliament was in iession, which decided on a domestic policy involving the greatest monopoly this country has ever seen, and for the payment of hidden subsidies to a corporation whose civilian heads had had very little training. There was one exception, because the head of Trans-Canada Air Lines, Philip Johnson, had come from the United States, and was an able business man who had had experience in aviation.
But Canada's policy of not calling an empire conference on civil aviation will have unfortunate results, because she has been advocating a policy of internationalization. No definition has been given with respect to what internationalization is, and no one understands what it is. The House of Commons has never seen this particular agreement, and I doubt if some of the dominions have ever

read it. I doubt if the British parliament has ever seen it or discussed it, because they had a debate over there last June.
Some forip of internationalization is no doubt necessary. Some form of private enterprise, or a mixed form of private and public enterprise, might be considered. But I believe the whole policy of the government is entirely wrong and a leap in the dark, and it is one which will not commend itself to the wisdom of the country. After all is said and done, if that is the view of the government, then there is very little hope for civil aviation in Canada in the future of Canada or the empire. I never have been able to see how this secret conclusion was ever reached. Civil aviation should not be a political question, nor should it be the plaything of any political party. It should be considered on its merits. In the great future which lies before this country we must wrap ourselves up with the mother country and the dominions, as a unit, in a joint empire air scheme, as we did in war.
As far as domestic aviation goes it is wrong to create a monopoly in this and other countries. The government is just drawing red herrings across the track, with a war on, and creating unnecessary dog-fights between these two companies. All this is being done when the war is not yet won. We should get back to basic things, namely, what the British empire as a unit should do in connection with civil aviation with an all-empire plan.
Instead of sticking to the main policy and the main task that is before us, instead of considering what is best to be done, we start off by creating a dog-fight between the two transportation systems in this country which have been doing glorious work in this war.
I was interested in civil aviation many years ago in connection with the policy of the present government and the government before it. Little or nothing was done, before the two wars, about civil aviation; it was left to private enterprise. The means by which we were able to obtain a technical victory in the battle of Great Britain were made possible by the information obtained in the Schneider race in 1931. The British government were able to obtain information which laid the foundations for the winning of the battle of London in 1940. The low-wing monoplane was born in that race, and this was the ancestor of the Spitfire and the Hurricane. Many great inventions followed out of the information obtained from those races. But there has been a complete lack of policy on the part of this government and that of the mother country in connection with civil aviation.

I am dissatisfied with the policy of this government because it will not solve the problem. The two transportation companies are to be put'out of existence in the air and all surface road transport, and a new company is to be substituted. They do not say how Canadian Pacific Air Lines are to be liquidated, and they fail to recognize the findings of the council of British shipping. This is an important body which has done much to help to win the battle of the Atlantic and keep the empire trade routes open in war. Their experience dates back for 200 years in providing sea services, and they outline the part they feel they can play in civil aviation. The report of that body in 1944 reads:
Our problem in this matter is greater, hut our opportunities are also greater than those of any other great power. The shipping industry does not pretend to any specialized knowledge of aviation, but it possesses experience of travel.
What it does possess and what it offers as a practical contribution to this task is a wealth of experience derived from our generations of successful management of overseas services; an efficient organization already dealing with those classes of passengers and freights likely to be borne by air; and a network of branch offices and agencies all over the world.
That contribution, the result of vast experience, W'as at first gained in monopoly before other countries took to overseas ventures, and then in competition with shipping subsidized by foreign governments. Having watched the effects of subsidies and of monopoly, the shipping companies believe that they should not be established for the air. They also believe that "persistent subsidy would retard genuinely healthy progress." ...
The war itself is both a forcing house for the development of the aeroplane and an agent for the wholesale destruction of ships. What might therefore have been a gradual, will become an abrupt transition. British shipowners, when tackling the rehabilitation of their traditional services after the war, will be presented also with an unusual opportunity to convert them spontaneously from the old medium to the new, in whatever respects and in whatever proportions their respective characteristics and the requirements of each trade or group of trades may suggest.
But any such spontaneous conversion is faced immediately by two obstacles. First, there is the risk under present legislation that shipowners may find themselves in competition with their qwn government in the shape of British overseas airways corporation.
This corporation holds a legal monopoly of all British services which are subsidized from public funds. The council of British shipping hold that their experience is of great value to the future.
A far wider and more varied deployment of experience, resources and individual enterprise would appear to be required, and British shipowners, in technique and experience and in their long established position in international transport, should be able to make certainly not

War Appropriation-Transport
an executive but a substantial contribution to the sum total of British air commerce. Ships and aeroplanes are by no means mutually exclusive. On the contrary, experience has shown that they can, and ideally should, be operated in a sense complementary to each other.
The conduct of a regular air line and that of a regular se& line have wholly systematic characteristics. Each calls for long term policies; each requires an international outlook; in each rigid technical discipline is essential to public safety; each finally succeeds only by capturing and retaining the goodwill of the travelling public or the consignor of freight.
In this remarkable memorandum the council of British shipping have made a real contribution to our understanding of the subject of air and sea transport. They end with suggesting that there should be a national empire board and they say;
In its twenty-five years of existence the national maritime board, on all questions of seagoing conditions and pay, has not only acquired confidence and authority, but has developed within itself a happy combination of mutual respect, eommonsense and an absence of rhetoric.
New Zealand and Australia have attempted to do something in connection with air routes and civil aviation. Mr. Curtin and Mr. Fraser appealed to Canada, last January when they met, to hold a meeting in order to bring about a unified policy for the empire. When I spoke on this matter here two weeks ago I quoted the speeches of Mr. Curtin and Mr. Fraser of January last and also referred to what the war correspondent of the Sunday Times said in his dispatch dated January 16. I repeat:
It is not generally realized at home that America has a Pacific air route which is marvellously well organized. On the day after war ends the same pilots, planes, air crews, ground organization, wireless and meteorological services will be available to begin commercial air services between Canada, America, Australia and New Zealand.
The British empire will not be in this lucrative traffic because nowhere on the Pacific route during war is there one British plane, pilot, meteorological expert or radio operator. Unless Britain places air crews on this route in 1944 she will be left at the post as far as experience and good will of services go, if peace comes in 1G45.
The Prime Ministers of Australia and New Zealand made an appeal to Canada to send delegates to an empire conference, and urged that serious consideration be given to the question.
The United States have been progressive in civil aviation. Many of the prominent men in this industry gained their experience in the R.A.F. in Toronto during the last war. The Americans have a tremendous hold over the Pacific, and they did not get it by accident but by enterprise, at a time when Canada
was asleep. They have made great concessions to travellers. The United States air service over the Pacific is free, every military or civilian traveller having the benefit of that route at no cost to himself.
The Prime Ministers of Australia and New Zealand had a conference on the 17th of January at which they agreed on an airways plan and made an appeal for an empire air policy. Canada has ignored it all, and has done nothing about it. Now Canada announces an international air policy as though she were a first-class power. I can tell you this, that America will have nothing to do with internationalization, neither will Russia. Russia has an agreement with the mother country for after the war to which the dominions are not a party.
I am very much disappointed with the whole air policy of the government, and I do not believe it will ever be consummated. In Canada we should have a chair in civil aviation in every large university, especially after the glorious record that Canada has made in this war with the empire training plan, which cost the taxpayers of this country close to a billion dollars. But we shall get little value out of it all under the domestic and international policies of this government. How does it come about that this policy is announced over the head of parliament and that a secret international document like this was produced in Washington over our heads and put into the record? It was done over the head of this parliament while in session, and over the head of the mother country, over the head of Australia and New Zealand and the other dominions which have been fighting with Canada in this war. Imagine the future for our young aviators coming back from this war if we have no settled air policy! This policy has been got up by a minister of the crown over the head of parliament. How many members have read this secret international proposed agreement? I have read it three or four times and I as a simple Canadian citizen am shocked by it. It gees over the head of Britain, which stood alone in the battle of Britain. This policy is got out over the head of parliament while our young aviators are fighting overseas. I doubt if few members have read the policy. It is, in my opinion, a shock to the people of the empire, and I have made a study of civil aviation ever since the magnificent record Canada made in the air in the last war.
I have waited for over twenty years for this day, to see that civil aviation would at least get a break here and that we could have
War Appropriation-Transport

a discussion in this house of this matter. Hitherto we have had no chance to discuss the future of aviation and the place it will occupy in our life when our young men come back from the war. How many of them, when they return, will have one hundred dollars in their pockets to finance a feeder line? What is the use of talking about their coming home as o-wners to enter an air industry? They will have twenty-five dollars in their pocket to buy a suit of clothes, but not sixty dollars, and yet we have squandered millions on camps all over this country without suitable sewers or water in them. Is that what our pilots are fighting for? Is that what we are doing for them, instead of calling a conference with the other dominions with a view to action along the lines I have indicated?
We have a navigation policy under which any ship can enter our harbours and land its cargo. They cannot enter our coastwise trade on the Atlantic or Pacific, but they can land their goods at our ports. That policy has proven in navigation a success for two hundred years, and has made Great Britain the great ocean-going country she is. The same principle should be applied to civil aviation, which should be free the world over. I regret that, instead of sticking to the large issue, the government has brought in these irrelevant matters when the war is on, and at a time when the railways are doing magnificent work they are to be deprived of any share in civil aviation. At a time when railway facilities in this country are choked, the ministry says: Nobody shall engage in civil aviation except the government, and they shall have a monopoly of it. I am not a Canadian Pacific man or any other kind of man, but one of independent mind, but I do say that this policy is a mistake. The government has got out a political feport on civil aviation in the domestic and in the international field. Civil aviation should rank next ,to agriculture in providing work and employment for our young men when they return from this war after writing the most glorious page in the lpstory of the world. I still have ten to fifteen minutes, Mr. Chairman, and I will continue my remarks when this question comes before us again, since I see it is now eleven o'clock.
